exp.0:1:
Paul wishes the believers in Corinth grace and peace. Grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is the calm and reconciliation that He gives. Both come from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes together with Timothy to the church in Corinth and to the believers throughout all of Achaia. It was a common greeting in his letters. Here it matters, because his relationship with the Corinthians had been strained, and he writes to them with affection and sincerity before speaking about comfort in the midst of suffering.

For today: before speaking with someone you have difficulties with, ask God for grace and peace for that person and for yourself. Beginning with a kind attitude can open the door to a healthy conversation.
exp.0:3:
He tells us that God comforts us in all our tribulation, and that this comfort does not stop with us. We receive it so that we can encourage others who are going through any kind of distress, using the same comfort that God gave us.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with Timothy at his side. Before speaking of his own sufferings, he praises God as the Father of mercies. Then he explains that his afflictions and his comfort also serve to strengthen the Corinthians.

For today: if God sustained you in a difficult moment, do not keep that story to yourself. Think of someone who is suffering something similar, draw near, listen to them, and humbly tell them how God comforted you.
exp.0:7:
Paul says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be unaware of the trouble he went through in Asia. It was a burden far beyond the ordinary, so heavy that it went past his strength. It was so severe that he doubted whether he would come out of it alive.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom his relationship is at times strained. He has just spoken of the comfort God gives in suffering. Now he honestly shares his own ordeal. We do not know with certainty what it was; scholars have proposed different ideas, and the text does not make it clear. What is clear is that Paul reached his limit, and that God delivered him.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. Paul admitted his weakness before others. If you are overwhelmed, tell God and a trusted person. That is where comfort can begin.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that he and his companions felt in themselves that they already had a sentence of death. This happened so that they would stop trusting in their own strength and place all their trust in God, who raises the dead. The word "sentence" here means a verdict or judgment.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them about a very hard trouble he went through in Asia, so heavy that they doubted they would come out alive. We do not know with certainty exactly what it was; scholars offer different ideas. What matters to him is that God delivered them, and that the Corinthians can help by praying.

For today: when you feel without strength or without a way out, do not see it as the end. It may be an invitation to let go of control and rest in God. Bring your situation to him in prayer, and ask others to pray with you as well.
exp.0:9:
He delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver us; in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us. This verse says that God rescued Paul and his companions from a danger of death so great that he continues to do so, and that they trust he will do it again.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them that in Asia they went through a trial so severe that they nearly gave up hope of living. We do not know exactly what that affliction was; various ideas have been proposed, but the text does not make it clear. Paul explains that this experience taught them not to trust in themselves, but in God, who raises the dead. He also asks them to pray for them.

For today: when you remember how God sustained you through past trials, let that strengthen your trust for what lies ahead. Write down those times and give thanks for them, and do not stop asking other believers for prayer.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that what fills him with a healthy pride is having a clear conscience. He affirms that he has lived with simplicity (plainness, without hidden motives) and with godly sincerity (honesty that comes from God). He did not rely on worldly wisdom, that is, on human cleverness or tricks for persuading people, but on the grace of God. This is how he behaved in the world, and even more so toward the Corinthians.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, with which he had a strained relationship. Some were questioning his motives and his conduct. Just before this, he spoke of his sufferings and of how God had delivered him. Here he defends himself with humility, appealing to his conscience and to what the Corinthians had already seen in him.

Today, strive to live so that your conscience is clear before God: be transparent in your words and decisions, and do not depend on appearances or cunning, but on his grace.
exp.0:21:
It says that God himself has marked us with a seal and gave us the Holy Spirit as a pledge. A pledge is a down payment or guarantee: a first installment that assures the rest will come. The seal shows that we belong to God and that he protects us. All of this takes place in our hearts, that is, in the innermost part of the person.

Paul speaks here, writing to the Christians in Corinth. He had been criticized for changing his travel plans, and people accused him of not being firm in his word. He answers that God is faithful and that it is God who sustains all of us in Christ. That is why his word is not careless.

For today: when you doubt your faith or your future, remember that your security does not depend on your own strength, but on the fact that God has sealed you and given you his Spirit. Rest in that and live with confidence and gratitude.
exp.1:2:
Paul says he wrote that letter so that he would not arrive in Corinth and find sorrow where he expected joy. He trusted that his joy was also the joy of all of them, meaning that they shared the same desires and rejoiced together.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth, with whom he had a strained relationship. He had had to correct them, and this pained him. He preferred to do it by letter rather than with another painful visit, to give them time to change. Scholars debate which letter this is, but the meaning is clear: he was moved by love, not anger.

For today: when you have to say something hard to someone you love, do it with care and with time, seeking their good and the restoration of the relationship, not winning an argument.
exp.1:4:
If someone caused sorrow, he did not grieve me alone, but in part, and, to avoid overstating it, he grieved all of you. The word that the source uses for "caused grief" means made someone sad or caused pain. The phrase about not burdening you means that Paul did not want to press too hard or make the matter sound worse than it was.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. Someone in the community had committed a serious offense, and the whole church suffered for it. Paul avoids presenting himself as the only one wounded, and he does not want to load anyone with blame. Scholars debate who that person was and what the exact offense was, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when someone hurts us within the church or the family, let us remember that the pain is rarely ours alone. Let us speak with moderation, without exaggerating the offense, and seek correction that leads to forgiveness and restoration.
exp.1:5:
It says that for that person, the punishment he received from the majority is already enough, or sufficient. Paul says it has already been enough.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after an earlier letter, written with tears, in which he asked them to correct someone who had caused pain. The man's name is not given here, nor his exact offense, and scholars do not agree on who he was. Most of the church had already corrected him, and Paul asks them now to forgive him and comfort him.

For today: correction should aim to restore, not to humiliate forever. If someone has repented and has already faced the consequences, offer him forgiveness, support, and an open door to walk again with the community.
exp.1:6:
Paul asks the Corinthians to do the opposite of punishing now: to forgive and comfort that person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a painful moment. Someone caused hurt, and the community gave that person a rebuke by majority. It is not known with certainty who this was or what the exact offense was; scholars interpret it in various ways. What is clear is that the punishment has already done its purpose, and now it is time to restore.

For today: correction should not be the end of the story. If someone has repented and has already been corrected, help them get back on their feet with a kind word, a hug, or an invitation. Forgiving and comforting is also a way of obeying God.
exp.1:11:
Paul tells how he came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ. There a door had been opened for him, that is, a good opportunity to proclaim the message. The phrase breaks off here and continues in the next verse.

The one speaking is Paul, writing to the Corinthians after a strained relationship with them. He was deeply worried about how things were going in Corinth and was waiting for news from Titus. So, although there was an opportunity in Troas, he had no peace and went on to Macedonia looking for him.

For today: an open door does not always mean that everything is in order in our hearts. When something troubles us, such as a broken relationship, it is wise to deal with it through prayer and wisdom, trusting that God is still at work.
exp.1:13:
Paul gives thanks to God because He always leads us in triumph in Christ. Moreover, through us He makes the knowledge of God spread everywhere like a pleasing fragrance.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians after a period of strain with them. He had just described his distress in Troas, where he did not find Titus, who was bringing news from Corinth. Even so, he suddenly praises God. The image seems to be drawn from a victory procession, although some scholars understand it in other ways. The central point is that the triumph belongs to Christ, not to Paul.

We can trust that God works even in moments of worry or apparent failure. Our task is not to draw attention to ourselves, but to live and speak of Christ with sincerity and kindness, so that others may perceive something of his goodness in us.
exp.1:14:
For we are a sweet savour of Christ to God, and this fragrance reaches everyone: those who are being saved and those who are perishing. The phrase "those who are perishing" refers to people who reject the message of the gospel.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a difficult time, and he tells them that he was anxious because he could not find Titus. Even so, he thanks God because his ministry moves forward like a victory procession. Some understand the image of the fragrance as the incense of those Roman processions, though this is interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that Paul speaks of his service and of how the message is received in different ways.

For today: live and speak with sincerity, without boasting or manipulating others. Not everyone will respond well, and that does not mean you have failed. Your task is to be faithful to Christ, and God takes care of the outcome.
exp.1:16:
Paul says that he and his companions are not like the many who corrupt the word of God. Those who corrupt it are false traders, people who sell it or water it down to make a profit. The image may suggest a merchant who mixes or dilutes his goods. By contrast, they speak with sincerity, as those sent by God, aware that he sees them, and in union with Christ.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, and he has just spoken of the great responsibility of proclaiming the gospel, asking who is sufficient for such a task. He answers that it does not depend on their own strength or on personal gain. He is probably defending himself against criticism and against other teachers who sought benefit. Scholars debate exactly who they were, but the contrast with his own ministry is clear.

For today: before you teach or share the Bible, ask yourself what your motive is. Speak with honesty, without twisting the message to please people or to gain something, remembering that God is listening.
exp.2:0:
Paul asks the Corinthians two questions. He asks whether he is beginning again to commend himself, and whether he needs, as some others do, letters of recommendation to you or from you. The word "commend" here means to praise or recommend oneself, and "letters of recommendation" are letters that introduce and vouch for a person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, the church he himself helped to bring into being. He had earlier been accused of boasting, and there were teachers who arrived carrying letters of endorsement. Paul does not need that: the changed lives of the Corinthians are his best proof. Commentators see here a touch of gentle irony.

For today: we do not need to boast about our service or seek applause. What speaks most about us is the fruit that God produces in our own life and in the lives of others. Live in such a way that your testimony is your best letter.
exp.2:8:
The explanation says that the ministry of condemnation, that is, the law of Moses that exposed sin and declared people guilty, came with glory. But the ministry of righteousness, the gospel that declares us righteous before God, has a much greater glory.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some teachers were questioning his authority. He compares the ministry of Moses, with the law engraved on stone and the shining face, with the ministry of the new covenant. He does not despise the law, which was also glorious, but he affirms that the grace of Christ surpasses it.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's acceptance through your own effort. Receive each day the forgiveness and righteousness that Christ has already given you, and let that gratitude move you to obey him with joy.
exp.2:9:
It says that the law given at Sinai, which did have glory, now barely shines when it is compared with the much greater glory of the new covenant.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his ministry against those who questioned it. He compares the ministry of Moses, the law written on stone, with the ministry of the Spirit, which gives life and righteousness in Christ. He does not say the law was bad; he says its glory was temporary and prepared the way for something greater.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of rules to keep. Trust in what Christ has already done, and let the Spirit transform you, with gratitude and without fear.
exp.2:12:
Paul says that he does not act like Moses, who covered his face with a veil. According to the text, Moses did this so that the Israelites would not keep their eyes fixed on the end of what was going to be set aside, that is, what was going to be brought to an end and no longer hold force. The glory on Moses' face was temporary.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry. He compares the old covenant, given through Moses, with the new covenant in Christ, which is more glorious and lasting. For this reason he preaches openly, hiding nothing. Interpreters explain the exact purpose of the veil in different ways, but Paul uses it as an image of a truth that was not yet seen clearly.

Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, without pretending or hiding what we are. Let us ask Him to help us see Christ clearly throughout the Scriptures and to speak of Him with confidence and humility.
exp.2:14:
Paul says that even in his time, when the law of Moses was read aloud in the synagogues, something covered the hearts of the listeners. The "veil" is a picture: it means they could not grasp the true meaning of what they heard. The reading aloud refers to the public reading of Scripture.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and recalls that Moses covered his face after speaking with God (Exodus 34). He compares the old covenant with the new. Many Jews listened to the Scriptures, but did not see Christ in them. Interpreters explain the veil in different ways, but all agree that the lack of understanding is taken away when a person turns to the Lord.

We can read the Bible with humility and ask God to open our understanding. Reading alone is not enough; we need to look for Christ in its pages, and He gives us light and freedom.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that the Lord is the Spirit, and that where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. "There" means in that place or in that life. The liberty here is the one God gives, not the freedom to do whatever one wants.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. He compares the reading of the law of Moses, which many Jews heard with a veil over the heart, that is, without understanding Christ, with the new life in the Lord. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. Some interpret the phrase "the Lord is the Spirit" to mean that Christ and the Spirit act together, without Paul saying that they are the same person.

Today, if you feel bound by guilt, fear, or empty religion, come to God with sincerity. Ask him that his Spirit give you understanding and liberty to live in his truth and love.
exp.3:1:
Paul says that he and his companions have turned away from hidden and shameful things. He speaks of secret places to hide in, and of cunning or trickery. They do not manipulate or distort the message of God; instead they set out the truth plainly, so that every honest and sincere person can weigh it in the sight of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some doubted his integrity and his ministry. He maintains that his service is the fruit of God's mercy, and so he does not lose heart. His way of preaching is open and without tricks, and this prepares what follows about those who cannot see the gospel.

For today: teach and live your faith with transparency. Do not adjust or dress up God's message to please people or to gain advantage; let your conduct be seen without fear.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that the same God who commanded light to shine out of darkness at creation is the one who has shone in our hearts. That light gives us the knowledge of God's glory, which can be seen clearly in the face of Jesus Christ. The word "face" here means the countenance or presence of Jesus, and "shine" means that something becomes clear and understood.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. Earlier he said that the god of this age (many understand this to refer to Satan) blinds unbelievers. Paul makes clear that he does not preach himself, but Christ. Later he will say that he carries this treasure in clay jars, that is, in fragile people.

For today: if understanding God is God's own work, we can pray with humility, asking him for light, and look to Jesus to know him better. We can also share what we know of Christ without boasting, remembering that the light comes from God.
exp.3:14:
Paul says that everything he endures, he endures for the sake of the Corinthians. His aim is that God's grace reach more and more people, so that the thanksgiving offered to God grows as well, and God is glorified.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had experienced tensions. He defends his ministry and explains that his sufferings do not defeat him, because he trusts in the resurrection. His difficulties serve so that others may know the gospel and receive the grace of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we see our difficulties only as a burden or also as an opportunity. When we serve with patience and faith, even in the midst of weariness, God can use us to bless others. And every blessing received is one more reason to give thanks.
exp.4:6:
We believers say that we live and make decisions by trusting God and his promises, and not only by what we can see with our eyes. Our way of living day to day is guided by faith, and sight refers to what can be seen or confirmed right now.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them that while we live in this body, we do not yet see the Lord face to face, and so we are away from him. Even so, God gave us his Spirit as a guarantee of what is to come. For this reason Paul is encouraged and confident, even in the face of death.

When you face a difficult situation and see no way out, you can take the next step trusting that God is faithful. Pray, seek his guidance in the Bible, and act with integrity, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.4:10:
Paul says that the fear of the Lord controls him, and for that reason he tries to persuade people. Here "fear" means a deep, reverent respect toward God, not a fear that paralyzes. Being moved by that respect is what drives him. God sees his heart clearly, and Paul hopes that the consciences of the Corinthians will also recognize him as sincere.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had doubted his honesty and his ministry. He has just reminded them that everyone will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. For that reason he insists that his way of serving is open and that his motivation is to please God, not to impress people.

For today: live out and share your faith knowing that God knows your motives. Before you speak or serve, ask yourself: "Am I doing this to please God and truly help, or to look good?" Ask him to keep your heart sincere.
exp.4:11:
Paul says that he is not trying to commend himself to them again as someone trustworthy. Rather, he wants to give them reasons to be proud of him, so that they can answer those who boast in outward things and not in what is within. Commending oneself means recommending oneself, and boasting means taking pride in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers criticized him and questioned his authority, relying on his appearance, their letters of recommendation, and their eloquence. Paul has just spoken of the judgment seat of Christ and of God knowing his heart. For that reason he does not defend himself out of pride, but so that the church will not be deceived. Some interpret that there is a touch of irony; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can learn not to judge or admire people only by their outward image or visible success. Let us ask God to teach us to look at the heart, beginning with our own.
exp.5:3:
He says that Paul and his companions seek to show themselves in every way as true servants of God. They demonstrate this by enduring with great steadiness (persistence, not giving up) the hardships, the lacks, and the situations with no way out. The word that describes how they conduct themselves can be rendered as behaving or carrying themselves as God's servants.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, with whom there was tension and doubt about his ministry. In the previous verse he asks not to give any cause for stumbling, so that the gospel would not be criticized. For this reason he presents his conduct and his sufferings as proof of his sincerity. A long list of trials and virtues follows.

For today: our witness is seen most in how we respond when things become difficult. We can ask God for patience in a specific difficulty, and take care that our conduct does not hinder others from coming closer to Christ.
exp.5:6:
It says that Paul and his companions show themselves to be true servants of God in three ways: they speak the truth, they live with the power of God, and they use the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left. That means they are protected and equipped on every side, both to attack and to defend, with an upright life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted his authority. For that reason he presents his ministry as evidence: he endures beatings and imprisonment, yet he remains steadfast. His character and the power of God, not fame, are his credentials.

For today: in trials, defend your faith with an honest and just life rather than with arguments. Before answering a criticism, ask yourself whether your words are true and whether your actions reflect God. Ask him for his strength to do so.
exp.5:9:
Paul and his companions go through sorrow, yet they have a joy that does not go out. They are poor, yet through their service they make many rich spiritually. They have nothing in a material sense, yet they possess everything in Christ. The word "sorrowful" means full of grief; the phrase about making many rich is understood as giving spiritual riches to others.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted him. That is why he describes his ministry through contrasts: he suffers, but he does not lose hope. Right after this, he opens his heart to them and asks them to answer him with the same closeness.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can weep and, at the same time, rest in Christ. That joy does not depend on circumstances, but on what you already have in God. Ask him to renew it in you today.
exp.5:10:
He says that Paul speaks to the Corinthians with complete frankness and holds nothing back. Speaking freely and honestly is what it means to speak openly. Their heart being enlarged means that his affection is wide, with plenty of room for them.

Paul writes to a church with which he had had tensions. He has just described the sufferings of his ministry, and now he shows them his affection. In the verses that follow, he tells them that the problem is not a lack of love on his part, but that they are closed off. He asks them to respond by opening their hearts to him too, as children would.

For today: if there is a cold or strained relationship, take the first step with sincerity and warmth. Speak with clarity, without bitterness, and leave room in your heart to be reconciled.
exp.5:13:
It says that believers should not join in a close and unequal relationship with the unbelievers, that is, with those who do not believe in Christ. The "yoke" was the wooden piece that joined two animals so they could plow together. Paul asks, using images of contrast, what righteousness and unrighteousness have in common, or what light has to do with darkness.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, whom he loves as his children. He asks them to open their hearts, and then he warns them against partnerships that would pull them away from God, since they are the temple of the living God. Interpreters debate whether he has in mind marriage, business, or idolatry; he probably includes several areas.

Today, before you commit to a partnership, a relationship, or an important project, ask yourself whether that union will bring you closer to God or pull you away from him. That does not prevent you from loving and treating everyone well.
exp.6:2:
Paul makes clear to them that his earlier words were not an accusation. He tells them that he carries them so deep in his heart that their bond would not be broken, not even in death or in life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. He asks them to receive him again with confidence, because he has not wronged anyone. He had corrected them firmly before, and now he wants them to know that he did it out of love and not out of anger. The verses that follow show his relief and his joy over them.

For today: when you have to correct someone, make clear that you do it because you value them. A correction given with love heals; one given with contempt wounds. Guard your words and your attitude.
exp.6:3:
Paul says that he has great confidence in the Corinthians and that he takes pride in them. He is filled with comfort, and his joy overflows, despite all his afflictions.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had had tensions. He asks them to welcome him again with openness, assuring them that he never harmed or deceived them. Shortly before, he had sent them a firm letter, and now Titus brought him good news about how they received it. That is why his spirit changes, even though he had been very distressed.

For today: even in difficult times, we can find comfort in seeing that God works in other people. Today, encourage someone with specific words of appreciation.
exp.6:7:
Paul says that the letter he wrote to them caused them sorrow. He had felt regret for sending it, but now he no longer regrets it, because he sees that the sorrow lasted only a short time and brought something good.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. He had sent them a firm letter to correct them, and he feared he had hurt them too much. Titus has just arrived with good news: the Corinthians had been grieved and wanted to do what is right again. Many think that letter is different from 1 Corinthians, although there is no full agreement.

A correction given with love may hurt, but sometimes it is the path to healing. If someone corrects you sincerely, do not harden yourself right away; ask God for humility to listen. And if you must correct someone else, do it with kindness, truth, and a desire to help.
exp.6:9:
The explanation says there are two kinds of sorrow. The sorrow that is in line with God's will is the pain we feel when we see that we have failed Him. That sorrow moves us to change direction, and it brings salvation and leaves nothing to regret. The sorrow of the world, by contrast, is the sorrow that produces death.

Paul writes to the Corinthians after having sent them a harsh letter to correct them. At first he doubted that he had hurt them, but now he rejoices, because their sorrow led them to change. Many believe the letter refers to a problem of discipline in the church, though it is not known with certainty what it was.

For today: when you feel bad about a mistake, ask yourself whether your sorrow draws you closer to God and moves you to correct yourself, or whether it only sinks you into guilt or wounded pride. Bring your failure to God and take a concrete step of change.
exp.6:10:
Paul reminds the Corinthians what the godly sorrow produced in them: earnestness (care), a desire to clear themselves (defense), indignation against wrong (anger), reverence for God (fear), a longing to restore the relationship (strong desire), enthusiasm for doing what is right (zeal), and a willingness to correct the wrong (vindication, that is, to set things right). At the end he says that in this matter they proved themselves to be clear, meaning free of blame for continuing to tolerate the wrong.

Paul had written them a strong letter about a sin the church had tolerated. Titus brought the news that they had repented, and Paul rejoices, not because they were sad, but because of the change that followed.

For today: when someone corrects us, let us not run away or defend ourselves with pride. Let us ask whether this is a sorrow that draws us closer to God and moves us to truly change.
exp.6:11:
Paul says that when he wrote his earlier letter to the Corinthians, his main purpose was not to point out the one who committed the offense or to defend the one who suffered it. He wanted them to see clearly how much he cared for them, and to see it before God, that is, in complete sincerity. Care means genuine concern and interest.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth after a strained relationship. He had written them a strong letter, which caused them sorrow, and Titus brought him good news that they had responded with repentance. It is not known with certainty who the offender was; scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: when you have to correct someone, examine your motive. Let it not be to win an argument or to punish, but to show genuine care for that person, as God would.
exp.6:15:
Paul says that he rejoices because he can have full confidence in the Corinthians. The word "rejoice" means joy, and "confidence" means that he feels assurance and hope in them. The word "you" refers to the Corinthian believers themselves.

Paul writes this letter to a church with which he had tensions. He had sent them a strong letter of correction, and Titus brought him good news: they received it well and showed obedience. Paul had already spoken well of them to Titus, and this proved true. For that reason he ends this topic with relief and joy. It is an expression of reconciliation.

Today we can learn to encourage others with sincere words of trust. If someone has corrected their course or has improved a relationship, let us acknowledge that change with gratitude, instead of continuing to remember only the past. Expressed trust can strengthen the one who receives it.
exp.7:4:
It says that the Christians of Macedonia gave far more than Paul and his companions had hoped for. First they gave their own selves to the Lord, and then they put themselves at the disposal of the apostles, according to the will of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish a collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who gave generously even in the midst of poverty. Paul explains that their generosity came from having first given themselves to the Lord.

For today: before asking how much to give, ask yourself whether your heart is truly surrendered to God. When He has first place in your life, giving with joy, time, money, or service becomes a natural response and not a burden.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the Corinthians already excel in many good things: in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in eagerness and effort, and in their love toward Paul. So Paul encourages them to excel also in this grace, which here refers to generosity in giving.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He speaks to them about the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who gave with great sacrifice. He makes clear that he is not commanding them, but inviting them to show a sincere love.

For today: it is not enough to have good words or good knowledge of God. Ask yourself in what concrete way you can give with joy, according to your means, to help someone who is in need.
exp.7:14:
Paul quotes Scripture to say that when God provides, no one is left without what they need. Whoever gathered much did not have anything left over, and whoever gathered little did not come up short.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to help the poor believers in Jerusalem with an offering. He is asking for fairness: not that they would go without, but that they help now, so that at another time they themselves might be helped. The quotation comes from Exodus 16:18, when God gave the manna in the wilderness.

Today, if God has given you more than you need, ask yourself whom you can help with it. Sharing generously trusts that God cares for everyone.
exp.7:18:
He says that the brother known for his service in the gospel was not sent by Paul alone, but chosen by the churches to travel with them. His task was to carry the offering, which Paul and his team were administering to honor the Lord and to show the readiness of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to finish a collection for the believers in need in Jerusalem. He explains that Titus and another brother will go to help. The explanation does not say with certainty who this brother is; several names have been proposed, but the Bible does not make it clear.

For today: handle the church's money with transparency and with the help of several trustworthy people. In this way we protect our witness and give glory to God.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that he knows the eagerness of the Corinthians. He is proud of them and has told the Macedonians about it: that Achaia (the region of Corinth) had been ready since last year. Moreover, their enthusiasm stirred many others to take part.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had promised to help, but they had not yet finished. Paul praises them warmly and at the same time, gently, encourages them to complete what they began, so that their good witness does not remain only in words.

For today: a good intention needs follow-through. If God has placed in your heart the desire to help someone or to serve in some way, do not leave it pending. Set one concrete step this week and carry it out with joy. Your example can encourage others.
exp.8:3:
Paul says that if some Christians from Macedonia come with him to Corinth and find that the Corinthians do not have the offering ready, there would be shame. Paul would be ashamed, and even more so the Corinthians, for having spoken with such confidence about them. Paul's point is that the boasting he made about them would prove empty if the gift were not prepared.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He had praised them before the Macedonians for their good will. Now he sends some brothers ahead so that everything will be ready and the offering will be given generously and willingly.

For today: if we have promised to help someone, let us keep our word on time and from the heart. We can set aside what we offered, without leaving it until the last moment, so that our generosity is sincere and not a rushed obligation.
exp.8:9:
God is the one who gives seed to the sower and also bread for food. He himself will multiply what you sow and make the fruits of your righteousness grow, that is, of your good and generous deeds. The seed that is sown, or the field that is sown, and the increase, or the harvest, are the things the verse speaks of.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they were gathering for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He uses the image of the field: God provides what is necessary, and generosity produces a harvest that leads many to give thanks to God. Paul does not promise personal wealth, but that God will give enough for them to keep doing good.

Today we can give with confidence, knowing that what we have comes from God. Think of a specific need near you and share some of your time, money, or resources with joy.
exp.8:10:
God enriches us in every way, so that we can be generous on every occasion. That generosity, when it reaches others, leads them to give thanks to God. The phrase "thanksgiving" in the verse is the word that matters here, and it appears in the verse as "thanksgiving to God."

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to finish their offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God provides the seed and the bread, and that the offering not only helps those in need but also leads many to praise God.

For today: if God has given you something, whether money, time, or abilities, ask yourself whom you can bless with it. Give with joy and simplicity, trusting that God takes care of you, and let your generosity lead others to thank Him.
exp.9:1:
Paul asks the Corinthians that, when he comes to visit them, he will not have to be harsh or bold. He says he is determined to act with firmness toward certain people who think he lives according to the flesh, that is, guided by weak or self-interested human motives.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some critics said he was brave in his letters but weak and insignificant in person. He answers that his gentleness imitates Christ and is not weakness. He prefers to correct them now with love so that he will not have to do it with severity later.

For today: if you have authority, in the family, the church, or at work, try to correct first with patience and humility. And if you are criticized unjustly, do not respond with pride; respond with truth and gentleness, as Christ did.
exp.9:2:
Paul says that although he lives in a human body, weak and mortal, he does not fight his battles with human or selfish methods. The word "war" in the verse means to fight as a soldier does. "The flesh" refers to the way of thinking and acting of the world, marked by pride, manipulation, or self-reliance.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them accused him of acting out of human interests. They saw him as humble when he was present and bold when he wrote from a distance. He answers that his authority does not come from human tricks. In the verses that follow, he explains that his weapons have divine power.

For today: when you face a conflict, whether in the family, the church, or at work, do not respond with shouting, hints, or manipulation. Pray, speak the truth with respect, and trust that God works better than your pride.
exp.9:4:
This verse speaks of tearing down arguments and every proud thing that rises up against the knowledge of God. It also says that every thought must be brought captive, that is, made subject, to the obedience of Christ.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his authority as an apostle against those who criticized him and judged him by appearances. He explains that his struggle is not carried on with human methods, but with the power of God. The weapons he speaks of are a figure for truth, prayer and testimony, not for violence.

For today: when a thought of pride, doubt or resentment arises, pause and compare it with what Jesus teaches. Bring it to Christ in prayer and choose to obey him, even though at first it may be hard.
exp.9:5:
He says that Paul and his companions are ready to correct every act of disobedience, but first they wait until the obedience of the Corinthians is complete. Being ready means being prepared. "To punish" here is understood as correcting or disciplining with authority.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some questioned his authority and saw him as weak. He explains that their struggle is spiritual, not fleshly. Before acting with firmness, he gives the church time to respond well. Interpreters debate exactly what correction he had in mind, but his patience and his desire to build up, not to destroy, are evident.

For today: when someone needs correcting, let us do it with patience and with a desire to restore. And let us first examine our own obedience to Christ before demanding it of others.
exp.9:6:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they are judging only by what meets the eye. He then points out that if anyone feels confident that he belongs to Christ, he should recognize that Paul and his companions belong to Christ too.

Paul writes to a church where some people criticized him and doubted his authority, perhaps because of his appearance or his way of speaking. He answers them firmly but with affection. His authority comes from Christ and seeks to build up the church, not tear it down. Interpreters do not fully agree on who these critics were, but the complaint is clear.

Today, before judging someone by their appearance, their style, or the way they speak, stop and ask what is in their heart and their faith. Christ unites those who belong to him, even when they look very different.
exp.9:7:
Paul says that, even if he boasts a little more about the authority the Lord gave him, he will not be ashamed. That authority has a clear purpose: to build up the faith of the Corinthians, not to tear them down. Paul's own word for boasting, which the verse renders as boast, means to take pride in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some criticized him and doubted his authority as an apostle. They said his letters were strong, but that in person he was weak. Paul defends his calling without attacking for the sake of it, and makes clear that his goal is to help them grow, even when he has to correct them.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in the family, the church, or at work, use it to lift others up and not to humiliate them. Correct firmly when necessary, but with the desire that the person grows.
exp.9:11:
Paul says that he does not dare to put himself in the same group or to compare himself with certain men who commend themselves. Those people use their own yardstick to measure themselves: they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves among themselves. Paul concludes that this is not having understanding; in other words, they are not wise.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had tension. Some were criticizing him, saying that his letters were strong but that in person he was weak and spoke without impact. In response, he uses irony about those who recommend themselves, and he explains that his authority comes from the task God gave him, not from his own opinion.

For today: do not use your own standard or comparison with others as the measure of your worth or your service. Ask yourself what God has entrusted to you, and be faithful in that, with humility.
exp.9:12:
Paul says he will not boast beyond what is rightly his. He rejoices only in what God assigned to him, and that includes having reached the Corinthians.

Paul is answering some people in Corinth who criticized him, saying he was bold in his letters but weak when he was present in person. Others were praising themselves and comparing themselves with one another. Paul does not join that game. He affirms that God gave him a field of work, and that Corinth fell within that field because he preached the gospel to them first.

Today we can learn not to compare ourselves with others or boast about what others do. Ask yourself what God has entrusted to you: your family, your work, your church. Serve it with humility, and be thankful for what He does through you.
exp.10:1:
Paul says he feels a holy jealousy for the Corinthians, a care that comes from God himself. He uses the image of a wedding: he has promised them in marriage to one husband, Christ. His hope is to present them in the end as a pure bride, that is, faithful and without stain in their love for him. Here "jealousy" means an intense and protective concern, not envy.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself founded. Other teachers have arrived who present a different Jesus and a different gospel, and Paul feels obligated to defend his ministry. That is why he asks them to bear with him even though it may seem foolish for him to speak about himself this way. He is worried that they will be led astray.

For today: examine whether your faith remains centered on the simple Christ of the gospel. Compare what you hear with what the Bible says, and guard your loyalty to Jesus above passing trends or attention-grabbing teachings.
exp.10:2:
Paul says he is afraid that the Corinthians may be deceived, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness. He fears that their minds may be corrupted and drawn away from the sincerity that is in Christ: a wholehearted devotion, without mixture or entanglement.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth, whom he himself brought to the gospel. He describes himself as a father who betrothed them to Christ as a pure bride. He is concerned that some teachers who came later may present them with a different Jesus and a different gospel, and that they may accept them far too easily.

Today, when we hear new or very striking teachings, it is wise to compare them with what Jesus has already shown us in the Bible. If an idea complicates the faith or changes who Christ is, it should be examined calmly and in prayer before it is accepted.
exp.10:9:
Paul states with great seriousness: "As the truth of Christ is in me," that is, he speaks as someone who belongs to Christ and does not lie. He says that this boasting, or reason for pride, will not be stopped by anyone, that no one will take it away or silence him throughout the regions of Achaia, where Corinth was. That boast is having preached the gospel without charging the Corinthians anything.

Paul is writing to a church where some teachers presented themselves as superior to him. He had preached to them free of charge, and the brothers from Macedonia supplied his needs. Now he defends his conduct and affirms that he will continue the same way, so as not to give a pretext to those who criticized him.

For today: serve with generosity and without hidden self-interest. Take care that the way you serve does not hinder the gospel or give reason to doubt your sincerity.
exp.10:11:
Paul says he will keep doing what he has been doing: preaching to the Corinthians without charging them. In this way he removes the opportunity from those who look for one. He wants them to be found just like him in the very thing they boast about.

Paul speaks to the church in Corinth. He has served without receiving support from them, and some rival teachers used this to question his love and his authority. Paul states that his motive is love for them, and that none of this comes from contempt. He then calls those men false apostles. Scholars debate the exact details of what they intended, but the text shows that Paul did not want to give them any pretext.

For today: let us make sure that the way we serve is clear and honest, even when it costs us. Sometimes it is worth giving up a right so that the gospel is not hindered or open to suspicion.
exp.10:15:
Paul asks that no one think he is a fool. But if they do think so, then let them receive him even as a fool, so that he too may boast a little.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who were being influenced by false apostles who presented themselves as superior. To show who the true servant of Christ was, Paul finds himself forced to boast, something that makes him uncomfortable. He does it with irony, and in the verses that follow he admits that he is not speaking as the Lord would have him speak, but as one who is out of his mind.

For today: do not be impressed only by the one who speaks well or boasts much. Always compare what you hear with the Word and with the character of Christ. And if at some point you must defend your testimony, do it with humility and without pride.
exp.10:22:
Paul asks whether the other teachers are ministers of Christ, and he clarifies that he speaks as a foolish man would. Even so, he claims that he is more. He mentions more labors, beatings beyond measure, more imprisonments, and many times he was close to death.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers boasted of being superior and questioned his authority. He compares himself with them, but he does so with irony and reluctance, calling it foolishness. He does not boast of successes but of sufferings, to show that his service to Christ was real and costly.

For today: let us not measure Christian service by how impressive or successful it looks, but by faithfulness, love, and humble self-giving. When faced with someone who boasts a great deal, let us look for the fruit and character of Christ.
exp.10:24:
Paul lists some of the sufferings he endured for preaching Christ. He was beaten with rods three times, a punishment carried out by Roman authorities. He was stoned once. He suffered three shipwrecks, and he spent a night and a day in the deep sea, that is, in the middle of the waters, probably floating after a shipwreck, although the text gives no further details.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. Some proud teachers criticized him and boasted of their achievements. So Paul, with a certain irony, speaks as though he were a fool and boasts, but not of successes; he boasts of his weaknesses and of what he suffered in serving.

For today: serving God is not always easy or comfortable. When you go through hardships for doing good, remember that God sustains those who serve him, and that his strength is most evident when we feel weak.
exp.10:31:
Here Paul tells how, in Damascus, the governor who served under King Aretas placed guards over the city in order to seize him. The guards watched the gates, and the aim was to capture him.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth, who were being swayed by critics who boasted of their achievements. Instead of boasting of power, Paul recounts with irony a humiliating scene: he had to escape in secret. He says he will boast of the things that show his weakness. Historians debate how Aretas came to have control in Damascus, and there is no certain explanation for it.

For today: you do not need to appear strong to be useful to God. Your moments of weakness, fear, or shame can show that strength comes from Him. Be honest about your limits and trust in His care.
exp.10:32:
He says that Paul escaped from Damascus when people were looking to arrest him. They lowered him through a window that opened onto the city wall, inside a basket, which was a large wicker or rope basket. In this way he escaped from the hands of those who wanted to seize him.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians. Some were criticizing him and boasting of their own glories, so he answers by listing his sufferings as an apostle. He mentions this escape almost at the end of the list, and it is an unheroic scene: he does not flee with strength, but hidden and lowered down by others. Scholars understand that with this he shows that his boast lies in his weakness, where God's help is seen. This episode also appears in Acts 9:23-25.

For today: do not be ashamed of the moments when all you can do is escape, ask for help, or depend on others. God can care for you in your weakness too, and sometimes he uses ordinary people as his basket of rescue.
exp.11:1:
Paul speaks of a man "in Christ", that is, a believer, who fourteen years earlier was "caught up", carried away suddenly and forcefully, to the "third heaven". He does not know whether it happened in his body or out of his body; only God knows.

The one speaking is Paul, and almost everyone understands that he is talking about himself, although he tells it as if it were another person. He feels compelled to defend himself before some in Corinth who boasted of their spiritual experiences. About the "third heaven", it is thought to be the presence of God, but the text gives no further detail.

Today we can learn from Paul's humility. He kept this experience for fourteen years and did not use it to boast. If God gives us something valuable, it is not to show ourselves off, but to serve with simplicity and give glory to Christ.
exp.11:3:
This verse says that the man was "caught up", that is, carried away suddenly and forcibly, into paradise. There he heard unspeakable words, things that cannot be told or that a person is not allowed to repeat.

The apostle Paul is speaking. He almost certainly means himself, though he tells it as if he were speaking of another person. He does this because some in Corinth boasted of visions and spiritual superiority, and he answers with humility. Whether it happened in the body or outside of it, he himself does not know. Then he says he would rather boast of his weaknesses.

For today: you do not need extraordinary experiences to be valued before God. Paul chose to keep silent and not boast. Try to keep humility in your faith, trusting more in God's grace than in your spiritual experiences.
exp.11:4:
He says that Paul is willing to boast about that certain man who was taken up to paradise. But about himself he will not boast of anything, except his weaknesses, meaning his frailties and limitations. To boast means to take pride in something or to show off.

Paul speaks to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who bragged about visions and power. To defend his ministry, Paul recounts this experience in the third person, and almost everyone thinks he is referring to himself, though he does not say so openly. Then he mentions his thorn, which kept him humble. We do not know for certain what it was.

Today we can learn not to base our worth on impressive achievements or spiritual experiences. Simply acknowledging our weaknesses keeps us humble and shows that strength comes from God.
exp.11:13:
Paul says he is ready to visit the Corinthians for the third time. He reassures them that he will not be a burden to them, because he is not after their money or possessions but after them. He makes a comparison: children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents save up for their children.

Paul speaks as an apostle and as the founder of that church. Some in Corinth questioned his authority, and he defends himself with a note of irony, since he had not charged them anything. He presents himself as a spiritual father who gives without expecting payment, and his priority is their well-being.

For today: whoever serves others, in the church or in the family, should ask what they are seeking: what they can receive or the good of the people. True love gives first, without turning others into a source of profit.
exp.11:19:
Paul says he is worried about what he will find when he visits the Corinthians. He fears they will not be as he wants them to be, and that he will not be as they would want him to be, meaning he may have to correct them firmly. He lists problems: contentions (fights), envyings (jealousy), wraths (anger), strifes (divisions), backbitings (speaking badly of others), whisperings (gossip), swellings (pride and arrogance), and tumults (groups opposing one another).

Paul writes this letter as an apostle and the founder of the church in Corinth. He has just defended his own conduct and that of Titus, and he insists that he does everything to build them up. His desire is not to shame them, but for them to repent before he arrives. His tone shows the affection of a spiritual father, but also seriousness.

For today: examine your relationships in the church, your family, or your workplace. If there is gossip, pride, or resentment, do not wait for someone to confront you. Ask God for forgiveness, and seek peace with that person this week.
exp.12:1:
Paul reminds them of something he had already warned them about: when he comes to Corinth for the third time, he will not spare those who sinned earlier or the others who keep on in the same way. He says it as if he were present, although he is writing from a distance.

Paul writes to a church that had questioned his authority. Some doubted that Christ spoke through him. That is why he warns them firmly that he does not want to catch them by surprise: he prefers that they put things right before he arrives. Some scholars think he has a specific apostolic discipline in mind; the text does not give details.

For today: if there is something in your life that God has shown you, do not wait for the correction to arrive. Acknowledge it and put it right now, with humility, while there is still time.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that the Corinthians are asking for proof that Christ speaks through him. He reminds them that Christ is not weak toward them, but powerful among them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had been corrected several times. Some doubted his authority as an apostle because his presence seemed weak and plain. He warns that he will come a third time and that, if necessary, he will act firmly against those who continue in sin. His words are not from pride, but from pastoral care.

For today: before demanding proof from others, look at how Christ has already been at work in your life. Be humble before correction, because God often uses ordinary people to speak truth to us.
exp.12:3:
He says that Christ was crucified in weakness, meaning he allowed himself to be taken to the cross without defending himself with human power, but now he lives by the power of God. Paul says that he too is weak, as Christ was, but that he will live with Christ by that same power, for the good of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. The Corinthians saw his weakness and took it as a sign of failure. Paul answers that Christ's weakness on the cross did not prevent the power of God from acting. He also warns that, if he comes again, he will act with firmness.

For today: do not be afraid to recognize your limits. Your weakness is no obstacle to God. Place it in his hands and trust that he can work with his power in your life and through you.
exp.12:5:
Paul says that he hopes the Corinthians will come to recognize that he and his team have not failed the test.

Paul writes to a church that doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Just before, he told them to examine themselves to see whether they were in the faith. If Christ lives in them, that very fact confirms that Paul's ministry was genuine. He does not defend himself out of pride, but for their good.

For today: before judging others, examine your own faith honestly. Ask yourself whether Christ is really guiding your life, and be humble enough to receive correction.
exp.12:10:
Paul closes his letter with some final words to the brothers and sisters. He asks them to rejoice, to strive to grow toward maturity, to allow themselves to be comforted, to think in harmony, and to live in peace. He promises that the God of peace and of love will be with them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he has had tensions over divisions and failures in conduct. He writes from a distance so that he will not have to be harsh when he arrives, since his authority is for building up and not for tearing down. His farewell is warm and pastoral.

For today: if there are disagreements in your family or in your church, seek peace and humility first, rather than winning the argument. God accompanies those who work to live in harmony.
exp.12:11:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, a greeting kiss that expresses pure, brotherly and sisterly affection. He then adds that all the saints, meaning the believers who are with him, send their greetings to them.

Paul ends this letter, which was harsh in several parts, on a note of peace. He has just urged them to seek unity and joy. In that time, greeting one another with a kiss on the cheek was a common custom. The word "holy" sets it apart as a clean gesture, a sign of family in the faith, not any other kind of affection.

Today the form of the greeting matters less, since it varies from culture to culture, than its spirit. Think of someone in your church with whom there is distance or tension, and greet them with genuine warmth: a hug, a handshake, or a few kind words.
exp.12:12:
This verse is a closing blessing. Paul wishes the Corinthians to receive the grace (the undeserved favor) of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, that is, the communion or companionship that the Spirit gives.

Paul closes a strong letter, in which he corrects a divided church and was questioned about his authority. Even so, he ends with peace and affection. He mentions the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, one of the clearest blessings in the New Testament regarding the Trinity.

For today: before ending a difficult conversation at home, at church, or at work, bless the other person. Ask that God give them grace, love, and communion, even if you do not yet agree on everything.
exp.4:15:
It says that Paul and his companions no longer regard anyone by appearances, that is, by merely human standards: background, status, or outward look. The phrase "according to the flesh" means judging by the world's criteria. It adds that Paul once regarded Christ in that same way, but no longer. "Regard" here refers to valuing or understanding someone, not just dealing with them.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had tensions, since some boasted about outward things and criticized him. Earlier he explained that the love of Christ drives him, because Christ died for all. For that reason he changed the way he looked at people. Scholars debate whether he once thought of Jesus only as a human teacher or as a rival, but the point is that now he sees him as Lord and Savior.

Today, before judging someone by their appearance, their money, or their past, ask yourself: "How does Christ see this person, the one for whom he died?" Ask God for a more loving way of seeing.
exp.4:0:
Paul says that we can be sure of something: if our body, which is like a house or tent where we live on earth, is taken down, God has a building ready for us. The word "house" in the verse refers to the place where one lives, and the picture of a tent points to a temporary dwelling. That building is not made by human hands, and it is eternal, in heaven.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, and he is speaking about the sufferings and fragility of life. In the previous chapter he speaks of our outer self that is wasting away. He wants to encourage them not to lose hope. Interpreters debate whether that house is a raised body or a heavenly dwelling; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when tiredness, sickness, or loss weigh on you, remember that this life is not all there is. Rest in God's promise and live with hope and confidence.
exp.0:2:
Paul begins by praising God. He calls Him "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," that is, the Father of Jesus. He also calls Him "the Father of compassion," which means that tenderness and care come from Him. And "the God of all comfort": the one who gives encouragement and relief in any situation. "Blessed" here means "praised."

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Corinth, together with Timothy. He had already come through very hard times, and in the verses that follow he speaks of his afflictions. Before explaining his sufferings, he begins by giving thanks to God for having sustained him.

For today: when you go through a difficult moment, draw near to God in prayer and tell Him what you feel. He comforts. Then, look for a way to lovingly accompany someone who is suffering, sharing the comfort that you received.
exp.11:11:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that the marks of a true apostle were performed among them. These marks were carried out with great perseverance. They also included signs, wonders, and miracles, which are powerful works of God that go beyond the ordinary.

Paul writes in his second letter to the Corinthians. Some false teachers looked down on him and boasted that they were superior. That is why Paul, reluctantly, has to defend his authority, even though he feels foolish doing so. Notice that he speaks of perseverance first, and only afterward the miracles. For him, suffering endured is part of the proof.

For today: let us not measure a leader only by how impressive or striking he is. Let us also look at his character, his humility, and his endurance. And when we are called to serve, let us seek to be faithful and steady, trusting that God works through our weakness.
exp.10:29:
If it becomes necessary to boast, Paul says he will boast about his weaknesses. The word "necessary" here reflects the idea of something that must be done, and "boast" means to take pride in something. "Weakness" refers to whatever makes a person feel fragile or limited.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who boasted of their credentials and achievements. To answer them, Paul makes a list of his sufferings and of his care for the churches. Instead of showing power, he shows what serving cost him. Then he tells how he had to escape from Damascus, a story that is anything but glorious.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong in order to serve God. You can be honest about your limits and trust that God works in the middle of them. Today, share a real difficulty with someone and thank God for sustaining you.
exp.5:11:
Paul tells the Corinthians that the restraint is not on his side. He is not holding back his affection from them. The picture is of a cramped space: the Corinthians have little room for him in their hearts. "Bowels" points to the innermost part of a person, where feelings begin. In other words: "We have made plenty of room for you in our hearts, but you have pulled back in your affection toward us."

Paul is writing to a church that had grown cold toward him, partly because of criticism and doubts about his ministry. He has just spoken of his sufferings and his open heart. Now, like a father, he asks them to respond with the same openness. Some think this prepares his call to separate from harmful influences, but that is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if there is someone who has served you with love, such as a pastor or a relative, check whether your heart has closed because of pride or misunderstandings. Take the first step and make room for them again.
exp.2:6:
Paul says that the law engraved in letters on stone, which he calls the "ministry of death," came with glory. Moses' face shone so brightly that the Israelites could not gaze at it. That glory, however, was fleeting.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against those who questioned it. He compares the old covenant, based on the law that revealed sin and condemnation, with the new covenant, given by the Spirit who gives life. His argument is that if what came before had glory, what is new has even more.

For today: do not trust in keeping rules to earn God's favor. Ask the Spirit to transform your heart, and live thankful for the grace Christ has given you.
exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus, that is, someone sent by Him, and he makes clear that he holds this role by the will of God, not by his own decision. Together with Timothy, whom he calls "our brother," he writes to the church of God in Corinth and to all the saints throughout Achaia. "Saints" refers to the believers set apart for God.

Paul writes this letter to a church that he himself helped to found, but with which he had experienced tensions and criticism about his authority. For that reason he begins by reminding them where his calling comes from. Achaia was the region of Greece where Corinth was located. Including all the believers throughout the area shows that the message was meant for a wider community.

For today: God calls us to serve without placing ourselves at the center. We can act with humility, remembering that our place in his work is a gift, and walk alongside other brothers and sisters.
exp.3:10:
Paul says that we who are alive as followers of Christ are always consigned to death for Jesus' sake. This is no accident: the purpose is that the life of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal body. "Always consigned to death" means being in constant danger; "mortal body" refers to our fragile physical life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, defending his ministry. He has suffered persecution, beatings and dangers for preaching the gospel. He explains that, although he seems weak, the power of God is shown precisely in that weakness. In this way, his suffering serves so that others may receive life.

For today: when you go through trials or exhaustion from following Jesus, do not think that God has forgotten you. Ask him that, in the midst of your weariness, others may see his patience, his love and his hope in you.
exp.10:28:
Here Paul says that he identifies himself with others in their suffering. The reader sees "weak" and "led into sin" in the verse, so the explanations are written for those words. To be weak means to lack strength, whether in body or in faith. To be led into sin means to be drawn into wrongdoing or to fall away from what is right. To burn with grief speaks of an inward fire: pain, anguish, and deep concern for that person.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against teachers who considered themselves superior. Instead of boasting of successes, he lists his sufferings. After speaking of beatings, weariness, and dangers, he mentions his heaviest burden: the care of all the churches. His pastoral love made him feel others' struggles as his own.

For today: love those who suffer or stumble truly. Do not judge them from a distance; draw near, listen, pray for them, and walk alongside them with tenderness and patience.
exp.7:16:
Paul says that Titus did welcome Paul's appeal to visit the Corinthians, but he was also so eager to help them that he is coming to them on his own volition. "Appeal" means a request or encouragement; "eagerly" means with great attentiveness and readiness; "of his own volition" means he is going by his own choice.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor Christians in Judea. He had earlier said that God placed the same care for them in Titus's heart. In this way he shows them that Titus comes with a good attitude, and that the collection will be handled responsibly.

Today we can learn that serving God is not just doing what we are asked. We can ask Him to give us a willing heart, to help others with joy and on our own initiative, not out of obligation.
exp.7:8:
The verse says that you already know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though He was rich, for your sake He became poor, so that through His poverty you might become rich. Grace is a favor that no one has earned. The word "you" in the verse refers to the people Paul is writing to.

Many understand the riches of Christ as His glory with the Father, and His poverty as His humble coming. The riches we receive are spiritual: forgiveness and life with God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to finish a gift they had started to help other believers who were in need. He does not give them a command, but uses the example of Christ to encourage their sincere generosity.

For today: before you give or help someone, remember how much you have received from Christ. Look for a concrete way to give with joy, according to what you are able to do, without pressure or pride.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that when a person turns to the Lord, the veil that covers their understanding is taken away. Here, "turns" means turning toward God, and the veil is a picture of spiritual blindness that keeps a person from seeing the true meaning of the Scriptures.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and recalls that Moses covered his face after speaking with God (Exodus 34). Paul uses that image to say that many of his people read the law of Moses without recognizing that it pointed to Christ. Some understand "the Lord" as Christ, others as God in general, but the sense is very similar.

For today: if there are parts of the Bible you do not understand, come to Christ with humility and ask him for light. Reading Scripture while looking to Jesus opens the understanding and transforms the heart little by little.
exp.10:23:
Paul says that five times he received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one, which means thirty-nine lashes with the whip. In all, that came to 195 lashes, and this was only on those five occasions.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. Some false teachers were bragging about their credentials and criticizing him. Reluctantly, and saying that he speaks as a fool, he lists the sufferings he endured for Christ. Many believe he stopped at thirty-nine so as not to go beyond the limit set by the law (Deuteronomy 25:3), although the Bible does not explain this here.

For today: true service to God is not measured by success or appearance, but by faithfulness in the midst of difficulties. When you serve with love and it costs you, remember that God sees what others do not see.
exp.5:16:
This verse calls believers to come out from among certain people or practices, to live set apart, and to touch no unclean thing, that is, nothing that defiles. God promises, "I will receive you," meaning he will welcome them as his own. The commands "come out" and "be separate" are addressed to the whole church.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived surrounded by idols and a pagan culture. He has just said that they are the temple of the living God, and that Christ and Belial (a name for evil) cannot go together. Drawing on words from the Old Testament, Paul reminds them that God wants a people of his own. The next verse promises that God will be their Father.

Today we can ask ourselves what habit, relationship, or influence pulls us away from God. This is not about looking down on people, but about setting wise boundaries to guard our faith, trusting that the Father receives us with love.
exp.10:19:
The explanation says that the Corinthians put up with anyone who mistreated them: whoever enslaved them, exploited them, took advantage of them, exalted himself, or struck them in the face. The words "anyone who enslaves you" describe a person who dominates others and makes them serve him, and "exalts himself" describes someone who sets himself above others.

Paul writes to them with irony, because some teachers who presented themselves as superior to him had arrived in Corinth. Paul feels compelled to boast and speaks foolishly to show that they tolerated those men, yet doubted the one who had served them with love. Scholars debate whether the blow to the face was literal or a picture of humiliation.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we follow. A leader who controls us, uses us, or humiliates us does not reflect Christ. Let us test everything in the light of the Bible and seek humble guides who serve.
exp.11:12:
Paul asks the Corinthians, with irony, in what way they were treated worse than the other churches. The only difference, he says, is that he did not become a burden to them, meaning he did not ask them for money to support him. Then he says, "Forgive me this wrong!" which is to say, "Forgive me this offense." He says it with an ironic tone, like someone apologizing for having done them a favor.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his authority as an apostle against critics who looked down on him. He feels uncomfortable having to speak about himself, and for that reason he says that he has become a fool. Some think his decision not to charge them was disapproved of by some people in Corinth, but the text does not fully explain this.

Today we can learn that serving others out of love sometimes means giving up our own rights. We also learn not to take offense at someone who serves us generously, nor to measure their affection by what it costs us.
exp.10:27:
Paul says that, apart from all the external trials he has already described, he faces something every day that presses on him: the pressure of his concern for all the churches. The phrase "pressing on me" in the verse means that the burdens pile up and arrive all at once. The word for concern here carries the sense of attention, care, and sincere investment in others.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and feels obliged to defend his ministry, because some teachers were questioning him. Instead of boasting about his achievements, he lists his dangers and his exhaustion. Here he shows that his greatest weight was not physical, but his pastoral love for the communities he had helped bring into being in the faith.

For today: if you look after others, whether in your family, your church, or your work, it is normal to feel that weight. Do not carry it alone. Bring it to God in prayer and look for fellow believers with whom to share the task.
exp.8:4:
Paul says he thought it necessary to ask the brothers, Titus and his companions, to visit the Corinthians ahead of him. Their task was to help the church get ready the gift it had already promised. The verse speaks of making arrangements in advance, so that the gift is prepared before Paul arrives. Paul wants the gift to be a generous offering, not something given grudgingly or only under pressure.
