Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the gift for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had promised it earlier, and Paul had spoken well of them to the Macedonians. He did not want them to be unprepared when he arrived with the Macedonians, which would leave everyone embarrassed.

For today: if God puts it on your heart to help someone or support your church, decide early and prepare your help calmly. That way you can give generously and with a glad heart, without last-minute pressure.
exp.10:26:
Paul lists more of the hardships he faced while serving Christ: labor and toil, often without sleep, hunger and thirst, often without food, and cold and exposure. The phrase "often without sleep" describes the repeated loss of rest that came with his work. The phrase "often without food" points to going hungry again and again. "Exposure" refers to being left without enough protection from the cold.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some boasted of their standing. Paul, with irony and sorrow, does not boast of his successes but of his weaknesses, to show that his service was genuine and costly.

Today, this reminds us that serving God does not always look impressive or comfortable. If you are worn out or going without necessities because you are doing good, you are not alone. Seek to value faithfulness above appearance, and pray for those who serve quietly.
exp.8:12:
The verse says that the help the Corinthians send is a real proof of their faith. Those who receive it will praise God for two reasons: because they see that the Corinthians obey the good news about Christ, and because the Corinthians are generous toward them and toward everyone else. The wording "this ministry" points to this: the help given is service, the "obedient confession" is their open declaration that they believe, and the "generosity of your contribution" is giving from what they have.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to finish a collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He explains that this offering not only meets needs but also brings thanks to God. For Paul, true faith shows itself in concrete deeds. It also unites believers from different places.

For today: help generously someone in your church or community who is in need. Do it simply, so that your faith is seen in action and others give thanks to God.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that all of God's promises find their "Yes" in Jesus Christ. In other words, they are fulfilled and confirmed in him. That is why we also speak our "Amen" through him, and this brings glory to God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because some were accusing him of changing his plans and of not being reliable. He answers that his message is not uncertain, wavering between yes and no, because God is faithful and Christ is God's firm answer. Then he says that God himself confirms us and gives us his Spirit as a guarantee.

For today: when you doubt that God will do what he has said, look to Jesus. Trust his promises and respond with a sincere "Amen," thanking him and living with hope.
exp.0:18:
The explanation says that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was proclaimed to the Corinthians by Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, and that in him there is no back-and-forth: he is not "Yes" and "No" at the same time. Instead, in him it has always been "Yes," meaning firmness and faithfulness. Here "proclaimed" simply means announced publicly. "Silvanus" is the same person as Silas.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some accused him of being unreliable and of saying whatever suited him. He answers that his message does not change, because Christ does not change. He defends his integrity by relying on the faithfulness of God.

For today: work to make your word trustworthy. Keep what you promise and, if you have to change a plan, explain it honestly. And when you doubt God, remember that in Jesus you always find a firm "Yes."
exp.12:0:
Paul says this is the third time he is getting ready to visit the Corinthians. Then he cites an old rule: every matter is to be confirmed by the testimony of two or three witnesses. "Matter" here means an issue or a case, and to be "established" means to be made firm or settled.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had conflicts. Some doubted his authority, and others were still living in sin. He uses the rule from Deuteronomy 19:15 to warn that, if he comes and there are accusations, he will deal with them justly. Scholars debate whether the "witnesses" are his visits or his warnings, or whether the phrase refers to the people who would give testimony. Even so, the general meaning is clear: he wants a fair process.

For today: before accusing or judging someone, seek out the facts and listen calmly. Do not repeat rumors. If there is a conflict, work to resolve it with truth, humility, and order.
exp.6:0:
This verse calls us to cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, that is, our actions and also our thoughts and attitudes. "Defiles" means makes unclean or impure. "Perfecting holiness" means continuing to grow in a life set apart for God, and "the fear of God" is respect and reverence toward Him. We are asked to do this "since we have these promises."

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth. The promises he refers to are in the previous chapter (6:16-18), where God says He will dwell among His people and be their Father. Then Paul asks them to receive him warmly, since he has wronged no one. Some scholars see here an invitation to separate themselves from the pagan practices of the city.

Today, if God promises us His nearness and His care, we can respond with gratitude. This week, identify one habit or thought that pulls you away from Him and ask Him for help to leave it behind.
exp.12:6:
Paul and his companions pray to God that the Corinthians will not do anything wrong. But they do not pray this so that they themselves will look successful, or so that others will see their ministry as proven. They pray it so that the believers will do what is right, even if that makes Paul appear to have failed.

Paul writes to a church that doubted his authority and wanted proof that Christ spoke through him. Before visiting them, he asks them to examine themselves. He would rather they put things right, so that he does not have to correct them harshly, even if that leaves him without proof of his authority.

For today: seek the good of others without thinking about your own image. If you help, correct, or advise someone, ask yourself whether you are doing it so that they grow in Christ or so that you look good. Pray for that person with that heart.
exp.11:20:
Paul worries that when he comes back to Corinth, God may humble him in front of them, and that he will have to grieve over many who sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery. Impurity is moral uncleanness, sexual immorality is sexual behavior outside of marriage, and debauchery is conduct that shows no restraint or shame. The words "sinned earlier" point to sins that had already been committed before Paul wrote.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church he himself founded. He is preparing for his third visit, and he speaks to them directly, not to defend his own reputation, but to build them up. The unrepentant sin of others grieves him more than his own humiliation would. His sorrow is that of a spiritual father who loves his children.

For today: do not minimize sin or hide it. If God is showing you something in your life, repent soon. And if you see a fallen brother or sister, approach them with tears and love, not with contempt.
exp.6:14:
He says that Titus feels a very deep affection for the Corinthians. The word "affection" points to the deepest feelings of the heart. That affection grows when Titus remembers that all of them were obedient and welcomed him with fear and trembling. The phrase "with fear and trembling" does not speak of being afraid of a person, but of seriousness and humility in receiving someone sent with an important message.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a tense relationship with them. He had sent Titus, and Titus returned encouraged by how they responded. Paul is glad because what he had said about them turned out to be true. Some understand the obedience as obedience to Paul and his letter; the text does not detail this further.

For today: when someone corrects you or serves you with good intentions, receive them with humility. And when you see good responses in others, express your affection and gratitude to them.
exp.8:8:
This verse quotes Scripture to show what a generous person is like. "He has scattered abroad His gifts" means he has distributed freely and widely, like someone scattering seed. "He has given to the poor" means he has given to those in need. And "His righteousness endures forever" means that his good work, his upright life before God, is not lost.

The quotation comes from Psalm 112:9.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and encourages them to take part in the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God loves the person who gives cheerfully and that He Himself supplies what is needed so they can give. Here he uses the Psalm as an example of what God approves.

For today: decide in your heart on one concrete way to help someone in need, without pressure or sadness, trusting that God takes care of you while you take care of others.
exp.11:16:
Paul asks: "Did I exploit you through any of the men I sent to you?" It is a question that expects the answer "no." To exploit someone here means to take unfair advantage of them through deceit, especially where money is concerned.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians and defending himself. Some were accusing him of being crafty and of having manipulated them, perhaps by charging them through the co-workers he sent. Paul had decided not to be a financial burden to them. So he appeals to what they themselves saw: Titus and the brother who went with him acted with the same spirit and the same steps as he did, that is, with integrity.

For today: live with transparency, especially in how you handle money and in your service. If someone doubts your intentions, respond with clear actions and with humility, always seeking to build others up and not defending yourself out of pride.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that he and his companions share the same spirit of faith that the psalmist had. The psalmist wrote, "I believed, and therefore I have spoken" (Psalm 116:10). Paul applies this to himself and his companions: because they believe, they also speak.

Paul writes to the Corinthians in the middle of suffering and danger for preaching Christ. He has just said that they are given over to death for Jesus. Even so, their faith does not fade, and for that reason they keep proclaiming the good news. Their hope is that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise them.

For today: if you truly believe in Jesus, your faith can come out in words. Even when you go through trials, take courage to speak simply of what God has done in you, whether with a friend, your family, or in prayer.
exp.4:1:
Because we live in a fragile body, believers sigh with longing. "Groan" means to sigh with both pain and hope. To be "clothed with" our heavenly dwelling means to be covered with something new, like putting a garment on over what you already wear. The "heavenly dwelling" is the new, eternal body that God promises, compared to a house.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was going through trials, and he himself was suffering. He compares the present body to a tent, something temporary. Some understand that he is speaking of the resurrection; others think of an intermediate state after death. What is clear is that he wants to encourage them with hope.

For today: when weariness, sickness or pain weigh on you, do not hide your sigh. Bring it before God and remember that his promise is new life, not loss.
exp.7:1:
The explanation says that the churches of Macedonia went through a terrible ordeal, a time of real suffering. Even so, their joy overflowed, and their deep poverty did not stop them from giving generously. The word "generosity" here means openness of heart toward others, and the idea of giving "abundantly" means they gave a great deal, even though they had very little.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to take part in a collection for the needy Christians in Jerusalem. To motivate them, he holds up the Macedonians as an example (including those in Philippi and Thessalonica). Paul credits that generosity to the grace of God, not to their wealth.

For today: do not wait until you have plenty to be generous. The joy that comes from God can move your heart to share, even when you have little, even in hard times.
exp.3:6:
The explanation says that the apostles have a very valuable treasure: the light of the knowledge of God's glory in Jesus Christ. But they carry it in jars of clay, that is, in fragile bodies, like simple clay jars. The jars are the containers that hold the treasure, and the fragility of the human body makes it clear that the strength is not ours. The power that is so great and surpassing comes from God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were used to admiring brilliant speakers. He reminds them that he does not preach himself, but Christ. Right away he speaks of his sufferings: afflictions, persecution, and being cast down. His weaknesses do not hinder the message; rather, they show that God is the one who sustains.

For today: when you feel tired, limited, or flawed, do not hide your weakness or wait until you are perfect in order to serve. Offer God what you are and trust that his power works through you.
exp.0:12:
Paul says that his letters contain nothing hidden or different from what the Corinthians can already read and understand. He hopes they will understand him completely, and he hopes that understanding will last to the end, that is, until Christ returns or until his relationship with them comes to an end.

Paul is writing to a church where some doubted his sincerity, since he had changed his travel plans. Earlier he said he had acted with "simplicity and godly sincerity." Here he argues that his words are clear and consistent, without double intentions. Some scholars see a wordplay in the Greek between "read" and "understand," but that is an interpretation.

For today: make sure your words and your actions match. Speak with clarity and honesty in your family, your work, and your church, so that those who know you find no hidden surprises in your character.
exp.1:7:
Paul asks the Corinthians to reaffirm their love for this person. Here, to reaffirm love means to show it clearly and openly once more. "I urge you" is Paul's warm appeal to them. He does not give a cold order, but pleads with them to welcome the person back.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about someone who had been disciplined by the community. The person's name is not given, and scholars discuss whether this is the man from 1 Corinthians 5 or another case. What is clear is that the punishment was already enough, and now the person is very sad. Paul wants them to be forgiven and comforted.

When someone admits his mistake and repents, it is not enough to say "I already forgave you." We can show love through actions: a kind word, an invitation, a hug, and so help that person feel again like part of the family.
exp.7:5:
He says that Paul and his companions urged Titus to help complete the work he had already started among the Corinthians. "Grace" here refers to the generous gift to help other believers. "Urged" means to encourage earnestly, and "complete" means to finish it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. The Christians of Macedonia, though they were poor, had given with joy for the needy saints in Jerusalem. Titus had already begun this collection in Corinth, and Paul wants them now to bring it to completion. He does not command it, but invites them warmly to show a sincere love.

For today: if you have started something good, such as helping someone or supporting a cause, do not leave it half-done. Ask God for steadiness, and finish it with joy and sincere love.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that whoever is united to Christ is a new creation. The old way of living without God, centered on oneself, has passed away, and something new has begun. The word "behold" can be read as "look" or "notice."

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Corinth. He had just explained that Christ died and rose again for everyone, so that we would no longer live for ourselves. For this reason he says that we no longer judge anyone by outward appearances. He then adds that this change comes from God, who reconciled us to himself.

For today: if you are in Christ, your past does not define who you are. You can ask God for help in leaving behind an old habit and living this week with a more generous and reconciling heart.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that Christ died for all, and that his death has a purpose: that those who now live should no longer live only for themselves, but for Jesus, who died and was raised again for them. The word "that" points to this purpose, and "but" sets up the contrast between living for oneself and living for him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. He says that the love of Christ moves him, and that this love "compels" him, meaning it presses him and guides him with force. Because Christ died for all, those who trust in him share in his death in some way and begin a new life. Some understand "all" as the whole of humanity, others as all believers.

Today, before making a decision, we can ask ourselves: "Is this only for me, or does it honor Christ and serve others?" Living grateful for his love changes our daily priorities.
exp.10:18:
Paul speaks with irony here. The Corinthians think they are wise, yet they gladly put up with fools. The word "put up with" means to endure or tolerate, and "gladly" means with pleasure. It is a gentle but firm rebuke.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which he founded. Some "super-apostles" came boasting of their achievements and questioning Paul. He feels compelled to boast as well, though he calls it "foolishness," to show how absurd that kind of pride is. The verses that follow explain that the Corinthians were enduring abuse from these leaders.

For today: do not admire someone simply because they speak with confidence or boast of success. Examine with humility, in the light of the Bible, what they teach and how they treat people, and do not tolerate abuse in the name of spiritual authority.
exp.6:4:
When Paul and his companions arrived in Macedonia, they had no rest. Their bodies were worn out, and here the word refers to their whole selves. They were pressed hard from every direction. Outside there were conflicts, meaning struggles and disputes, and inside they felt fears, that is, dread and worry.

Paul is speaking, writing to the Corinthians. He tells them honestly how hard his journey was while he waited for news from them. He had sent Titus and was anxious about how things would go for them. The next verse shows that God comforted him with Titus's arrival and his good news.

For today: you do not need to pretend to be strong. Paul admitted his fears with honesty. You can bring God your struggles from outside and your fears from within, and also let other believers be the means of comfort that He sends you.
exp.4:19:
Paul says that believers are ambassadors for Christ. An ambassador represents a ruler and speaks on his behalf. So it is as if God himself were making his appeal through them. "We implore you" means that Paul is asking earnestly and tenderly. The meaning is that you should return to peace with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had a difficult relationship. Shortly before, he explained that God had already taken the first step: in Christ he did not count people's sins against them. Now Paul describes his mission: to proclaim that message of peace. Some think he also calls the Corinthians to return to God; others see here above all a call to those who do not yet believe.

For today: if God has reconciled us to himself, we can invite others with humility and love, without boasting or condemning. Think of someone close to you and ask God for an opportunity to share his love with simple words.
exp.4:7:
Paul and his companions are full of courage and confidence. Even so, they would prefer to leave this earthly body and be at home with the Lord. The phrase "would prefer" describes their desire, "away from the body" refers to leaving this life through death, and "at home with the Lord" means being close to Him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth in the middle of suffering and weakness. Earlier he described the body as a fragile tent. Here he explains that death does not frighten him, because faith leads him to expect Christ. Then he makes clear that, whether he is at home in the body or away from it, he wants to please the Lord.

For today: when you feel fear or weariness, remember that your hope does not end with this life. That hope is not an excuse to live without desire, but a reason to live today in a way that pleases Christ, with faith and confidence.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the more we suffer for following Christ, the more comfort we receive through Him. The "sufferings of Christ" are the hardships that come from belonging to Him and serving Him; some believe they also refer to sharing in his sufferings. To "overflow" means to pour out in great amounts, spilling over and growing. "Comfort" is encouragement, relief, and strength.

The apostle Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. He has just praised God as the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. Paul had gone through great trials in his ministry, and he explains that both his suffering and his comfort also serve to encourage the Corinthians.

Today, when you go through a trial because of your faith or because you are doing what is right, do not think that God has left you alone. Ask Him for His comfort with confidence, and then use what you received to encourage another person who is suffering.
exp.2:10:
The explanation says that the old covenant, the law given through Moses, had glory, but its glory was fading away. "What was fading away" refers to something coming to an end. By contrast, the new covenant, "that which endures," has a greater glory because it lasts forever. "How much greater" means that its glory is far beyond the other.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. Some teachers were pulling them back toward the law of Moses. Paul shows them that the law was good and glorious, but the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness in Christ surpasses it. Interpreters agree on the general idea, although they debate some details about how it applies to the law.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of requirements to earn God's favor. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let his Spirit transform you little by little.
exp.7:23:
Paul asks the Corinthians to show openly, in front of the churches, that their love is real. The word "show" means to make something visible, and "proof" means clear evidence. He also reminds them that he has been proud of them, and he wants that confidence to be backed up by action, not left as words only.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the gift for the poor believers in Judea. He is sending Titus and other brothers to help them finish that collection. He had spoken well of the Corinthians to other churches, and now he encourages them to back up those words with deeds.

For today: Christian love shows itself in concrete actions. Think of a nearby need, whether of a brother or sister or of your church, and help generously and sincerely, not to look good, but to joyfully do what you say you believe.
exp.12:9:
Paul writes this letter from a distance because he hopes the Corinthians will put things right before he arrives, so that he will not have to be severe with them when he is with them. The authority he refers to is the authority the Lord gave him, and it is meant to be used for building up the Corinthians. He has no interest in using it to tear them down.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, a community with which he had had tensions, since some there questioned his authority. In this farewell he asks them to change and to grow in maturity, and he reminds them that his purpose is not to impose himself on them but to help them grow in the truth.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, the church, or the workplace, use it to lift people up and not to humiliate them. And if someone corrects you with love, use that time to set right whatever needs fixing.
exp.0:13:
The Corinthians have already come to understand, though only in part, that Paul and his companions are people they can take pride in, and that they are people Paul can take pride in as well. Here "you may boast of us" is the reader's wording, pointing to a cause for pride or joy shared in both directions. This mutual pride will reach its full expression on the day of our Lord Jesus, when Christ returns and everything is made clear.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had experienced tension and misunderstanding. Earlier in the letter he has defended his sincere conduct and his integrity. Now he reminds them that, despite their doubts, there is a bond of mutual appreciation. Many readers understand that, by saying "in part," Paul acknowledges that not everyone in Corinth yet saw it this way.

For today: value those who have helped you in your faith and tell them sincerely that you are grateful for their lives. Also take care of your relationships in the church, remembering that what we do together will matter before Christ.
exp.4:12:
Paul and his companions act for God and for the Corinthians. In the Berean Standard Bible wording, "out of our mind" and "of sound mind" describe two opposite states. Being out of your mind means acting in a way others see as excessive or unbalanced, and being of sound mind means having a clear head and acting sensibly. If they seem excessive in their devotion, it is for God; if they are sensible and balanced, it is for the good of others.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some were criticizing him and boasting about outward appearances. The verse does not tell us exactly what "out of our mind" refers to. Some think he was speaking of intense spiritual experiences; others, that he was being accused of being a fanatic. What is clear is that, according to the next verse, the love of Christ was what moved him.

For today: serve God with sincere devotion, even when others do not understand, and treat people with clarity, patience and good sense. Ask yourself what the other person needs, not how it affects you.
exp.4:20:
Jesus, who never sinned, was treated as a sinner in our place, so that we might be declared righteous before God through him. The phrase "made sin" is usually understood to mean that he bore our guilt or was offered as a sacrifice for sin; interpreters explain it in several different ways. Becoming "the righteousness of God" speaks of being right with God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. He has just said that God, through Christ, reconciles the world to himself and that believers are his ambassadors. This verse explains the reason for the appeal: "Be reconciled to God." Reconciliation is possible because of what Christ did.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor by your own efforts. When you feel unworthy, remember that your standing before God rests in Christ. Come to him with confidence, and share that same message of peace with others.
exp.8:2:
Paul says that he is sending some brothers to Corinth so that the pride he has expressed about them in this matter would not turn out to be empty. "Boasting" here means a reason for pride, and "empty" means without real basis. "Prepared" means ready and set. He wants them to be prepared, just as he had already said.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem (the "saints"). He had spoken well of them to the Macedonians, and now he sends Titus and other brothers to help them finish what they had promised. He did not want his praise to end in embarrassment.

For today: if we have promised to help someone, let us follow through with order and joy. Making a concrete plan, instead of leaving it to the last minute, honors God and protects our witness.
exp.1:9:
When the church forgives someone, Paul also forgives him. And if he has forgiven anything, he did it for your sake, in the presence of Christ. The phrase "if I have forgiven anything" shows humility: Paul does not insist on personal offenses.

Paul writes to the Corinthians after a painful situation in which someone had caused trouble and the church had disciplined him. Now that this person seems repentant, Paul asks them to restore him with love and joins in their forgiveness. He does this so that they will not gain sorrow or Satan's deception, as the following verse says. Scholars debate who exactly that person was.

For today: when someone truly repents, let us not keep the punishment longer than necessary. Let us forgive with humility, knowing that Christ forgave us, and help restore the relationship.
exp.2:11:
Paul says that because we have such a great hope, we are very bold in how we speak. "Such a hope" refers to the glory of the new covenant, which lasts. "Very bold" means speaking openly and clearly, without hiding anything.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending his ministry. He compares the old covenant, given through Moses, with the new covenant in Christ and the Spirit. The old had glory, but it was temporary. The new is more glorious and lasts. For this reason Paul preaches openly, without a veil, unlike Moses, who covered his face.

For today: if your hope is firmly in Christ, you do not need to speak of your faith with fear or in secret. You can share it with simplicity, honesty and courage, trusting that God works in hearts.
exp.2:17:
It says that all of us who believe, with unveiled faces, reflect the glory of the Lord. As we look at him, the Spirit is gradually transforming us, so that we are being made more and more like Jesus.

The phrase "with intensifying glory" describes a change that grows over time, with each stage bringing more of his likeness into our lives.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and compares the old covenant with the new. He recalls that Moses covered his face with a veil, and he says that this veil is taken away when someone turns to the Lord. Now there is freedom to draw near to God. Some understand the reflection as an imperfect image; others understand it as the place where we are transformed.

For today: spend a few minutes each day looking at Christ in his Word and in prayer, without fear or excuses. Ask the Spirit to change you, and be patient: transformation is a process, not a single moment.
exp.5:7:
The explanation says that Paul and his companions serve God both through glory and through dishonor. It notes that "dishonor" means being looked down on, and that "slander" means false, damaging talk, though those words are not in the verse you are reading. They are viewed as imposters, meaning people accused of being frauds or pretenders, but they are genuine people, sincere and honest.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some questioned his authority and his honesty. In this passage he describes what true ministry is like: it goes through suffering and criticism, yet remains faithful. Paul does not defend himself with pride, but shows his character and his devotion to Christ.

For today: do not let praise puff you up, nor let unfair criticism sink you. Seek to live with integrity before God. If you are misunderstood, remain sincere and kind, trusting that God knows your heart.
exp.8:6:
The verse says that each person should give what they have decided in their heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. The reason is that God loves the one who gives with joy. The word "dador" in the explanation refers to the giver, and the decision the verse describes is one made beforehand, in the heart.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had promised an offering to help the poor believers, whom many understand to be those in Jerusalem. He reminds them to give generously and not stingily. He wants their gift to be voluntary and not a last-minute pressure.

For today: before you give, pray and calmly decide how much you can give. That way your offering comes from a grateful heart and not from guilt, pressure, or habit.
exp.6:6:
Paul says that Titus encouraged him not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort Titus himself had received from the Corinthians. Titus told him that the Corinthians longed to see Paul, that they grieved over what had happened, and that they cared deeply for him. All of this gave Paul even more joy. "Mourning" means grieving, and "zeal" means eager, heartfelt devotion.

Paul writes from Macedonia, worn down by pressures from outside and worries from within. Earlier he had sent the Corinthians a firm letter to correct them, and he waited anxiously to hear how they would respond. Titus came back with good news: the church had responded with repentance and warm affection toward Paul.

For today: God often comforts us through other people. We can be like Titus, bringing a word of encouragement to someone who is suffering. We can also receive correction humbly from those who love us, because it can bring healing and reconciliation.
exp.7:0:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth about something God has done in the churches of Macedonia. The phrase "we want you to know" is what Paul means here. The "grace of God" is his favor and his generous work, which could be seen in the lives of those churches. The grace "given to" them is God's gift to them.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, encouraging them to take part in a collection to help other Christians in need. To motivate them, he holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who were poor and suffering, yet still gave with joy, as the following verses show.

For today: generosity is a gift from God, not only our own effort. We can ask him to give us a willing heart, and to give joyfully according to what we have, without waiting to become rich before helping someone.
exp.2:7:
Paul asks a question that already carries its own answer: if the ministry of the law, carved in stone, came with glory, will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious? "Ministry" means service or work done for God. "Spirit" here refers to the Holy Spirit, who works in the new covenant.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his service against those who questioned it. He compares the covenant given through Moses, whose glory was temporary, with the new covenant, where the Spirit gives life. Some understand the "letter" as the written law without God's power to change the heart; this is how the text presents it.

For today: do not rely only on your own efforts to keep rules. Ask the Holy Spirit to transform you from within, and serve others trusting in his power, not your own.
exp.11:18:
Paul asks the Corinthians whether they have been thinking all along that he was defending himself to them. He makes clear that he speaks sincerely before God, in Christ, and not to win favor from people. He says that everything he has written, dear friends, is meant to build you up, that is, to strengthen you in your faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom had turned against him and accused him of deceit, even in how he handled money. He points to Titus and the brother he sent, who acted with honesty. His words are not aimed at protecting his own standing, but at the good of the Corinthians before he visits them again.

For today: when you correct or advise someone, examine your motive. Ask yourself whether you are speaking to win an argument or to help that person grow, and speak with sincerity before God.
exp.7:22:
He is Paul's partner and fellow worker among the Corinthians, and our brothers are messengers of the churches and bring honor to Christ. The words "fellow worker" name a helper who labors alongside another. The phrase "among you" means in your company, or working with you.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth while he arranges a collection to help believers in need. He explains who will carry that money, so that no one has reason to doubt them. He wants everything to be done openly, as he said in the previous verse: in the sight of the Lord and in the sight of people.

For today: if we handle money or responsibilities in the church, it is wise to do so with order, clarity, and trustworthy people. Honesty does not diminish faith; rather, it protects the good name of Christ.
exp.6:1:
Paul asks the Corinthians: "Make room for us in your hearts." He then gives three reasons they can trust him: we have wronged no one (harmed or treated anyone unjustly), we have corrupted no one (ruined them or led them astray), and we have exploited no one (cheated or taken advantage of anyone).

Paul writes to a church with which he had experienced tensions. Some doubted his integrity. That is why, after inviting them to live in holiness, he asks them to open their hearts to him. In the following verse he clarifies that he is not condemning them, but loves them deeply. His conscience is at peace.

For today: when a relationship grows cold because of misunderstandings, let us seek reconciliation with humility and openness. Living with integrity allows us to ask for trust without fear, and it also reminds us to open our hearts to those who love us and correct us sincerely.
exp.1:0:
Paul says he made a personal decision: not to visit the Corinthians again in sorrow, that is, in an atmosphere of pain and rebuke. "So I made up my mind" in the Berean wording expresses the same idea of a private resolve made within himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, whom he loved despite the conflicts. He had earlier sent them a firm letter to correct them, and he did not want another visit to become a new, painful confrontation. Some scholars think there was a difficult earlier visit, although the text does not say so with complete clarity. What is clear is his desire that his relationship with them be strengthened and that his joy be shared.

Today we can learn to correct others with love and wisdom. Before confronting someone, it is good to pray, to choose the right moment, and to seek restoration, not merely to be right.
exp.4:18:
It says that God was bringing the world back to himself through Christ. "Reconciling" means making friends again with those who had been separated. "Not counting men's trespasses against them" means that God does not hold people's wrongs against them or charge them with their guilt. And God has entrusted us with the message of reconciliation, to share it with others.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had a difficult relationship. He defends his ministry and reminds them that everything begins with God, not with human effort. The verses that follow describe him as an ambassador: someone who speaks on behalf of another and pleads with people to accept peace with God.

For today: if God has already taken the step toward us, we can live without fear or shame. We can also offer that same forgiveness to others, with kind words and patience, whether in the family, at work, or with a friend we have drifted away from.
exp.2:2:
Paul says that the Corinthians are a letter from Christ, the result of Paul's ministry, written by the Spirit of the living God and not with ink. This letter is not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth. Some were questioning his authority and asking for letters of recommendation. Paul answers that the best proof of his ministry is the changed lives of the people themselves. The "tablets of stone" bring to mind the law of Moses, and he contrasts that with the inward work of the Spirit.

For today: people can read our lives more than our words. Ask the Spirit to soften your heart, and let the way you treat others show who Christ is.
exp.9:15:
Paul says that his desire is to carry the gospel to places farther than Corinth, where no one has yet preached it. He does not want to step into the work that belongs to others and boast about what was already done in someone else's territory.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, and some teachers were criticizing him and taking credit for work that was not theirs. Paul answers that he stays within the field God gave him. He hopes that their faith will grow so that his work can reach further, and he ends by saying that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.

Today we can serve with humility, do well what God has entrusted to us, and rejoice in what others do, without competing or claiming the credit for what they have built.
exp.2:4:
It says that we are not capable on our own, not even of claiming that anything good comes from us alone. The word "competent" in this verse means able, having what is needed to carry out a task. Paul affirms that all his ability comes from God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some were questioning his authority. He answers that his ministry does not rest on letters of recommendation or on his own talents. The proof is the believers themselves, changed by the Spirit. That is why his confidence is in God, who made him a minister of a new covenant.

Today we can serve with humility and without fear. If God is the one who equips us, we need neither to boast nor to feel useless. Before a difficult task, pray: "Lord, I cannot do it alone, but you can."
exp.10:13:
We should not be surprised that there are false teachers who appear good, because Satan himself masquerades as an "angel of light," that is, as something good and bright. "Masquerades" means that he takes on an appearance and pretends to be what he is not.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, to whom he had preached the gospel. Others had arrived who presented themselves as superior apostles and criticized him. Paul says they are "deceitful workers" who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. His warning seeks to protect the church from deception.

For today: it is not enough that someone sounds pious, is pleasant, or speaks about God. Compare what they teach with the Bible, see whether they exalt Jesus, and look at the fruit of their lives. Ask God for discernment.
exp.10:21:
Paul asks three questions, and to each one he gives the same answer: "So am I." Hebrews, Israelites, and descendants of Abraham are three ways of saying that he belongs to the people of God, with their language, their history, and their inheritance.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were being influenced by certain teachers who boasted of their Jewish background and their credentials to gain authority. Paul says he is speaking as a fool because he does not enjoy boasting, but he does it so that they will not be deceived. Later he will show that his true credential is his sufferings for Christ.

For today: do not be impressed only by titles, appearance, or polished presentation in someone who teaches. Examine their character, their faithfulness to Christ, and their humility. And when you have to defend yourself, do it with simplicity, without seeking your own glory.
exp.5:17:
It says that God promises to be a Father to his people, and that they will be his sons and daughters. "Lord Almighty" is a title that stresses his total power. The wording here is the Berean Standard Bible's: "I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who lived surrounded by idolatry. He asks them not to join in practices that contradict their faith. To support this, he gathers several phrases from the Old Testament, and this verse seems to draw ideas from texts such as 2 Samuel 7:14 and Isaiah 43:6. Some scholars see here a loose quotation rather than an exact one. The promise follows the invitation to separate from what is impure.

Today, when you decide to step away from something that harms your faith, you are not alone. God receives you as a father receives his children. Obey with confidence in his care.
exp.1:10:
He says that Paul does not want Satan to outwit them and lead them astray. He affirms that the believers are aware of Satan's schemes, that is, his plans and tricks for bringing people down. The phrase "in order that Satan should not outwit us" means that Satan would gain the upper hand over us.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a painful situation, in which someone had been disciplined. Now he asks them to forgive that person and restore him. He says that he too forgives, in the presence of Christ. Paul sees that refusing to forgive could lead to division and excessive sorrow, and that this would open a door to the enemy.

For today: if someone wronged you and has repented, do not hold a grudge. Forgiveness is not weakness; it is a way of protecting unity and of leaving no room for the enemy's deceptions.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that he and his companions have a ministry, a charge to serve. Your verse says God in his mercy has given them this ministry. They did not earn it through their own merit. That is why "we do not lose heart" means they do not give up or grow discouraged.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom he has had tensions. Some questioned his authority and his way of preaching. Just before this, he spoke of the new covenant and the glory of the gospel. Now he explains why he remains firm despite the difficulties: his ministry comes from the mercy of God.

For today: when you grow tired of serving or of doing good, remember that God gave you that calling in his mercy. You do not depend on your own strength, but on his grace. Ask him for encouragement today and take the next step with humility.
exp.7:7:
Paul says he is not giving a command. He wants to test whether the love of the Corinthians is genuine, and he does this by comparing it with the earnestness of other churches. "Love" is the meaning of the word here, and "earnestness" refers to the sincere effort others have shown. To "test" something means to check that it is genuine.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Earlier he told them how the churches of Macedonia gave generously, even though they were poor. Paul does not force them, but he invites them to finish what they had already begun. When he speaks of testing, he is not accusing them; he is encouraging them to show by their deeds what they say they feel.

For today: love shows itself in concrete actions. Think of a promise of help you left unfinished and carry it out gladly, without anyone having to force you.
exp.11:14:
Paul says he is glad to give everything he has, and even himself, for the good of the Corinthians. The phrase "spend and be spent" means giving what he has and being used up completely for them. He also asks, with some sadness, whether his greater love for them will lead them to love him less.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where his relationship is strained. Some were criticizing him and questioning his authority. He did not charge them for preaching, and with irony he asks them to forgive him for that. He compares himself to a father who gives to his children, not to someone who seeks to get something from them.

For today: real love means giving without conditions, even when we do not receive the same affection in return. We can keep serving someone with patience, without charging them or expecting gratitude, trusting that God sees that love.
exp.8:11:
The explanation says that the help the Corinthians are preparing does more than supply the needs of the believers who are poor, who are called here "the saints." It also overflows in many expressions of thanksgiving to God. The phrase "this ministry of service" refers to the act of delivering this help. "Supplying the needs" means that it meets what is lacking. "Expressions of thanksgiving" are ways people show their gratitude.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to complete an offering for the Christians in need in Jerusalem. Many understand that there was scarcity there, although the text does not give all the details. Paul wants them to give with joy and to see that their generosity has a greater purpose: that God be honored.

For today: when you help someone in need, do it simply and with trust in God. Your help meets a need, but it can also lead others to thank God.
exp.4:4:
He tells us that God himself has prepared us for a new and eternal life, what Paul calls being "clothed upon," with a glorious body. As a pledge of that promise, God has given us his Spirit. The word "pledge" means a first payment or deposit: something that assures us the rest will come.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He is speaking about the frailty of the body we have now, which he describes as a temporary tent. He groans and suffers, but he does not lose hope. His confidence is not in himself, but in what God has already begun to do.

For today: when you feel tired or limited, remember that the Holy Spirit within you is God's promise that what is best is still to come. Rest in his faithfulness and not only in what you can see.
exp.8:13:
The explanation says that the believers in Jerusalem, when they receive the help, will pray for the Corinthians and feel affection for them. They will do so as they see the surpassing grace, that is, the extraordinary kindness God gave the Corinthians to be generous. Their prayers will express a deep and heartfelt affection, and the phrase "because of the surpassing grace God has given you" points to the grace God has given you.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to complete the offering for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He explains that their help not only meets needs, but also produces thanksgiving to God and unites believers from different peoples, Jews and non-Jews. Some scholars also see here a sign of unity between both groups, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: when you give or serve others, do it with humility, knowing that generosity comes from God. And when someone helps you, pray for that person. In this way the bonds of love in the church are strengthened.
exp.10:0:
Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with him for a little while as he speaks like a "fool." By "foolishness" he means boasting about himself, which he himself considers foolish. The words "put up with" are the same as "bear with," and "but" is the same as "yet." So the sense is: "I hope you will put up with this foolishness of mine, and you are already doing so."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church he himself founded. Some outstanding "super-apostles" were influencing them and questioning Paul's authority. To defend himself, he feels forced to speak of his achievements and sufferings, even though it makes him uncomfortable. He does it out of love and concern for them, as the following verses explain.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we let ourselves be carried away by impressive voices rather than by the simplicity of the gospel. Compare what you hear with what Christ teaches in the Bible, and listen humbly to those who truly care for you.
exp.9:8:
Paul says that he does not want it to seem as if he is trying to frighten the Corinthians with his letters. In today's language: "I do not want them to think I only write to scare them." The word "frighten" in the verse means to scare someone or make them afraid.

In this letter Paul defends his authority as an apostle. Some in Corinth criticized him, saying his letters were strong but that in person he was weak and unimpressive. He clarifies that the authority God gave him is for building up the church, not for tearing it down. His goal is to help them grow, not to dominate them.

For today: when we correct someone, let us do it to build up and restore, not to frighten or impose ourselves. May our words and our lives agree, and may love guide every piece of advice.
exp.9:0:
Paul says that he himself pleads with the Corinthians, appealing to the gentleness and kindness of Christ. The word "I" stands at the start of his sentence, and "I appeal to you" means "I plead with you." He describes his manner as gentle, and some say that when he is present in person he is humble, timid or weak, but when he is away, by letter, he is bold.

Paul writes to a church that he founded, but in which some were criticizing him and doubting his authority. They accused him of being strong only in his letters. He does not answer with pride, but by recalling the character of Christ. The verses that follow show that he prefers to correct with tenderness, although he is willing to be firm if necessary.

When someone criticizes or questions us, we can respond with the gentleness of Christ instead of defending ourselves harshly. Being kind does not mean being weak; it means being able to use firmness with humility and love.
exp.3:11:
Paul says that he and his companions are going through suffering and danger, a kind of daily dying, and that this brings life to the Corinthians. The phrase "is at work" means "is active" or "takes effect." The sufferings of the messenger serve so that others receive life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church with which he had a difficult relationship. He reminds them that preaching the gospel costs him a great deal: persecution, exhaustion, and the risk of dying. But he keeps going with faith, trusting that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise all of them. Some understand "life" as spiritual life; others also include the hope of the resurrection.

For today: serve others even when it costs you. A mother who stays up late, a patient teacher, or a volunteer who gives their time can be channels of life for others. Today, make one concrete gesture of giving for someone, trusting that God will bring fruit.
exp.0:16:
Paul asks two questions. He asks whether, in changing his travel plans, he acted carelessly or without serious thought. And he asks whether he makes his plans by human standards, so that he would say "Yes, yes" and also "No, no."

Paul is writing to the Corinthians. He had planned to visit them twice, but he did not carry out those plans as he had intended. Some in Corinth were probably accusing him of being inconsistent and unreliable. He maintains that his changes did not come from a divided heart. The verses that follow connect this with the faithfulness of God and of Christ.

For today: when you have to change a plan or cannot keep what you promised, explain your reasons with humility and sincerity. Work to make your word trustworthy, thinking before you promise and not out of simple convenience.
exp.5:1:
Paul says that God heard and helped his people at a time of favor. "Time of favor" means a time when God welcomes people and shows his kindness. "Day of salvation" is a day of rescue. "Helped" means assisted. Paul insists that this moment is now.

Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, where God speaks to his Servant. He writes to the Corinthians and urges them, together with his co-workers, not to receive God's grace in vain, that is, without it producing fruit in their lives. This letter follows a period of tension between Paul and that church, and that is why he insists that they respond to God. Some understand "now" as the age of the gospel; others, as an urgent invitation to that congregation.

Today it is not wise to put off what God is asking of you. If you sense his call to forgive, to return to him, or to change something, respond today with humility and trust in his grace.
exp.9:14:
Paul says that he does not boast beyond what belongs to him, nor claim credit for work that others have done. He hopes that the faith of the Corinthians will keep growing, and that as it does, his own influence among them will greatly increase, always within the area of work that God assigned to him. "Limits" here means the area of work that God gave him. "Increase" means that his work should reach further.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers praised themselves and took pride in the work of others. Paul answers that he did arrive in Corinth with the gospel, and that he does not take over the effort of others. His desire is to keep moving forward and to preach in places where Christ is not yet known.

For today: honestly recognize what God has entrusted to you, and do not dress yourself up with the work of others. Rejoice when others grow in faith, and remember that all credit belongs to the Lord.
exp.3:4:
Paul says that he and his companions do not announce themselves. Their message is that Jesus Christ is Lord. And they, instead of seeking honor, present themselves as servants of the believers, for Jesus' sake.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some questioned his authority and admired more showy teachers. Just before this, he speaks of how many do not see the light of the gospel because they are blinded. So he clarifies that his message does not revolve around his own prestige, but around Christ, and that his service is humble, not for showing off.

For today: before speaking about your faith or serving in the church, ask yourself whether you are seeking to be admired or seeking for Jesus to be known. Serve with humility and always point toward Christ.
exp.7:12:
Paul makes clear that he does not want others to be relieved while the Corinthians are left under strain. The words "relieved" and "burdened" in this verse describe ease or relief on one side and pressure or difficulty on the other. He is not asking for help that would leave them in need.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor Christians in Judea. He reminds them that God values a sincere willingness and what each person can truly give. His goal is equality: that today some help others, and tomorrow, if needed, the situation be reversed.

For today: give generously, but with wisdom and according to your means. Think of someone close to you who is going through need and help them with something concrete, without neglecting the basics of your own family.
exp.7:3:
Paul tells us that the believers of Macedonia earnestly pleaded with him for the privilege of sharing in this gift. For them, giving was a favor they were grateful to be allowed to do. Taking part in that help is what the verse describes as sharing in this service, and "the saints" are the Christians in need in Jerusalem.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish their offering. He holds up the churches of Macedonia as an example: they lived in affliction and poverty, yet they gave with joy. They themselves asked for the privilege of taking part, without anyone forcing them.

Giving is not only an obligation; it can also be a privilege. This week, think of a specific need of a brother or sister or of your church, and give with joy whatever you can, even if it is little. God looks at the heart with which we give.
exp.10:20:
Paul admits, with shame, that compared with the false apostles he seemed too weak to act that way, because he had not treated the Corinthians harshly. He then says that whatever others dare to boast about, he can match. He acknowledges that speaking like this is foolish, since he is only doing it to answer the boasting of others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some arrogant teachers were dominating and exploiting the believers, and the believers were putting up with it. Paul does not want to boast, but he feels he must, with irony, to defend his ministry and to protect the believers from these deceptions.

Today we can learn not to be impressed by someone who speaks with great confidence or abuses their authority. Let us measure everything by the humble character of Christ, and value sincere service more than the appearance of power.
exp.8:0:
Paul says there is no need to write to them about the "service to the saints," that is, the help or gift for believers in need. The phrase "there is no need for me to write to you" means it would be pointless for him to write, because they already know about the matter.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In the previous chapter he spoke of this collection, which many understand as help for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. Now he wants to encourage them tactfully, acknowledging their willingness, so that they finish what they started. The details of how the offering was organized are known only in part from the text.

For today: when someone already has a good willingness to help, it is wise to encourage them with kindness rather than pressure. And if we have promised to help someone, let us ask God for steadiness to carry it out with joy and order.
exp.3:13:
Paul is certain of something: the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus, and will present us together with you in His presence. "Certain" here means having full confidence. "Raised" means brought back to life.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth in the middle of suffering and persecution. He explains that his work brings exhaustion and danger of death, but that others receive life through the message he preaches. He quotes Psalm 116: believing and speaking go together. His hope in the resurrection gives him courage to keep preaching, and that is why he does not give up.

For today: when you are tired, sick, or discouraged, remember that your hope does not depend on what you see now. If God raised up Jesus, he will also keep his promise to you. That confidence helps you keep serving, speaking about your faith, and encouraging others.
exp.6:12:
Paul says that he and his companions were encouraged when they saw how the Corinthians responded. But what gave them the greatest delight was seeing Titus happy. Here "refreshed" means renewed and reassured, and "encouraged" means strengthened and comforted. Titus was refreshed by the way all of you treated him.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth after a strained relationship. He had sent them a firm letter to correct a problem, and they reacted with genuine sorrow and a desire to make things right. Titus carried that letter and returned with good news. Paul shares his relief and recognizes that Titus's encouragement was also a blessing.

For today: when someone corrects you with love, respond with humility and a willingness to change. Also, encourage those who serve others, since their work is often hard, and a good welcome can renew their spirit.
exp.0:23:
Paul says that he and his companions do not want to lord it over the faith of the Corinthians, as if they were in charge of it. "Lording it over" means dominating or controlling. Instead, they see themselves as fellow workers who contribute to the Corinthians' joy. He also reminds them that they stand firm because of their own faith in Christ.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had tensions. He has just explained that he did not go to Corinth so as not to cause them more sorrow or to have to correct them harshly. He wants to make clear that his authority as an apostle is not for pressuring, but for serving.

Today, those who teach or lead in the church, as well as parents or friends, can ask themselves: "Am I controlling, or am I helping others grow in their joy and in their faith?" Walking alongside others with respect, without manipulating them, strengthens people's trust in God.
exp.10:5:
Paul admits that he may not be a polished speaker, but he insists that he is not lacking in knowledge. He adds that he has made this clear to the Corinthians in every way possible, so that they know who he is and what his ministry has been like.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were being swayed by some teachers who presented themselves as superior and spoke with great skill. Some criticized Paul for the way he spoke. He does not defend himself out of pride, but to protect the church from a different message. Scholars debate exactly who those "super-apostles" were, but the context shows that Paul sets his own sincerity against theirs.

Today we can learn not to measure a message by how impressive the speaker is, but by their faithfulness to Christ and his Word. Good character and a simple truth are worth more than polished words.
exp.12:7:
It says that Paul and his companions cannot do anything against the truth; they can only act for it. The phrase "we cannot do anything against" means that they are unable to oppose the truth in any way. The sentence shows that their authority is subject to what is true and is not used to twist it.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he has had tensions. Some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Before visiting them again, he tells them that he is not looking to look good or to win an argument. He would rather they do what is right, even if he is seen as having failed the test.

For today: when you correct or lead others, seek to serve the truth and not your pride. Ask yourself whether what you say or do helps build up the person, even if it does not make you look good.
exp.7:21:
Paul says that he is sending, along with Titus and another brother, a third brother whose name he does not mention. Paul has seen this man show real earnestness many times and in many ways. Now his eagerness is even greater, because of the great confidence he has in the Corinthians.

Paul is organizing the collection for the poor believers in Judea. To avoid suspicion about how the money is handled, he sends a team of trustworthy people. We do not know for certain who this brother is; some have proposed names, but the text does not say.

Today, when we manage church resources or help others, let us do things with order and openness. Working as a team and being accountable to one another is not distrust; it is a way of caring for our witness and for the name of Christ.
exp.9:16:
It says that if someone wants to boast or take pride in something, they should do so in what the Lord is and has done, not in themselves. "Boast" means to show pride or take pleasure in something. The phrase "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord" is a command: it tells the person to boast in the Lord.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. Some there were bragging and comparing themselves to the leaders, and they questioned Paul's authority. He answers that he does not boast about the work of others, but hopes that their faith will grow and that the gospel will reach new places. This verse sums up a phrase Paul takes from the ancient Scriptures (probably Jeremiah 9:24).

When you accomplish something, whether at work, in your studies, or in service, give thanks to God and recognize that He gave you the strength and the opportunities. In this way you avoid pride and also envy toward others.
exp.2:3:
Paul says he has a firm confidence, and that this confidence is ours "through Christ" before God. He is not talking about self-assurance, but about a certainty that comes through Jesus. The phrase "before God" means "in God's presence."

Paul is writing to believers in Corinth. Some were questioning his authority and asking for letters of recommendation. He answers that the proof of his ministry is the people themselves: lives changed by the Spirit. That fruit encourages him to speak with confidence. In the verses that follow, he clarifies that his ability comes from God, not from himself.

For today: when you feel incapable or unsure about what God has entrusted to you, remember that your confidence rests not on your talents but on Christ. Serve with humility and courage, because God is the one who gives the ability.
exp.5:0:
Paul says that he and his companions are God's fellow workers. From that position they urge the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain. Receiving it "in vain" means receiving it without result, without it bearing fruit or changing how they live. The phrase "we urge you" means "we earnestly encourage you."

Paul writes to a church that had already believed, but that had problems and doubts about his ministry. In the previous chapter he spoke of reconciliation with God through Christ. Now he asks that this reconciliation be seen in actions. Some understand "God's fellow workers" to mean that Paul works alongside God; the context suggests this.

Today we can ask ourselves: is my faith only something I believe, or does it also change how I treat others? Today, for example, you can ask someone for forgiveness or help someone who needs it, as a grateful response to the grace you have received.
exp.4:13:
It says that the love of Christ moves us, presses us, and guides us, like a force that will not let a person stay still. "Compels" means to drive someone strongly or to leave them no real choice. Paul reaches this conclusion: since one died for all, all died. This last point is understood in several ways: that all of us were lost and needed his death, or that whoever trusts in Christ dies with him to their old life.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the Corinthians. He is defending his ministry against those who boasted in outward things. He explains that his devotion, which some considered madness, springs from the love of Christ and not from self-interest.

For today: before serving or correcting others, ask yourself what moves you. If the love of Christ motivates you, you will serve with more patience, humility, and steadiness, without seeking applause.
exp.10:14:
It is not surprising, then, if Satan's servants disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. They "masquerade," that is, they put on an outward appearance that makes them look like something they are not. And the phrase "their end will correspond to their actions" means that in the end they will receive what they deserve for what they did, not for how they looked.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and he is defending his ministry. Some preachers came calling themselves apostles and discredited Paul. He calls them false because they deceived the church with an appearance of godliness. Many scholars see here a serious warning about who teaches and how they live.

Today it is not enough for someone to speak well or seem pious. Let us compare what they teach with the Bible and look at their fruit: humility, truth, and love for Christ.
exp.1:8:
Paul says that one of his reasons for writing his earlier letter was to see whether the Corinthians would stand the test and be obedient in everything. The idea here is of checking their faithfulness through a test, to find out what they truly were.

Paul is speaking to the believers in Corinth. It is thought that he is referring to a case of church discipline, perhaps that of a man who had done something serious. Now that this person was sorry and deeply saddened, Paul asks them to forgive and comfort him. Scholars do not fully agree on who this person was or which letter this was, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: obedience to God includes both correcting with truth and forgiving with love. If someone has repented, ask yourself whom you need to comfort and restore, instead of keeping them at a distance.
exp.3:8:
He says that although Paul and his companions suffer persecution, God does not leave them alone. To be "forsaken" means to be left behind, abandoned. To be "struck down" means to be hit and knocked to the ground, and yet they are not destroyed. To be "destroyed" means to be ruined or brought to an end.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and defends his ministry. He says that he carries the treasure of the gospel in fragile jars of clay, that is, in frail bodies. In this way it is clear that the strength comes from God and not from them. His sufferings unite him to Jesus, so that the life of Christ may be seen in him.

When you go through rejection, exhaustion, or hard blows, do not confuse weakness with abandonment. You can fall without being destroyed. Tell God honestly what you feel and rest in the knowledge that his power sustains you, even in your most fragile days.
exp.0:17:
Paul says that God, who is faithful, knows that what he told the Corinthians was not a "Yes" and a "No" at the same time. That is, his message was not uncertain or changeable.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some accused him of being inconstant and of speaking lightly, making promises out of human convenience. He defends his sincerity and calls God as witness. Then he connects his message with the faithfulness of Christ, in whom God fulfills his promises.

For today: work to make your word trustworthy. Keep what you promise and, if you truly must change a plan, explain the reasons with honesty and humility.
exp.7:13:
At this moment, the Corinthians have more than they need, and Paul asks them to use that surplus to help the believers in need in Jerusalem. In this way, if one day the Corinthians find themselves in need, those same believers could help them in return. "Surplus" is what is left over; "need" is what is lacking; "meet" means to fill or cover what is lacking; "equality" is a fair sharing, where no one is left without what is necessary.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He is encouraging them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor brothers and sisters in Judea. He makes clear that he does not want them to be squeezed while others rest. He asks for generosity according to what they have, given with a willing heart. Some understand that Paul is speaking only of material help; the text shows it this way in this passage.

Today, if you have more than you need, think of someone close to you who is in need and help them with joy. Remember that all of us may need help someday.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that God, who comforts the downcast, encouraged Paul and his companions when Titus arrived. The word "downcast" here refers to those who are discouraged or low in spirit. The word "comforted" means "encouraged and gave relief."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He was in Macedonia, weary, with conflicts on the outside and fears on the inside. He was waiting for news of how the Corinthians had received his previous letter, which had been harsh. Titus arrived with good news that they had repented and held him in high regard. Paul sees in this the hand of God.

God often comforts us through people. If you are downcast, do not isolate yourself: accept the company of other believers. And you can be the one who brings encouragement to someone through a visit, a phone call, or a sincere word.
exp.0:15:
This verse lays out the travel plan Paul had in mind. He wanted to visit the Corinthians on his way to Macedonia, return to them from Macedonia, and then have them help send him on toward Judea. The phrase "to visit you on my way to Macedonia" means that Corinth was a stop before he moved on to Macedonia, and "to have you help me on my way to Judea" means that the Corinthians would support him as he continued his journey.

Paul writes this letter to a church that was criticizing him because he had changed his plans. Some accused him of being unreliable or of not meaning what he said. That is why he reminds them of his original intention: to visit them twice so that they would be encouraged. In the verses that follow, he argues that his word is sincere and trustworthy.

For today: when you have to change a plan, explain your reasons with humility and honesty. And when someone changes their plans, do not assume the worst right away. Clear and kind communication helps protect trust.
exp.11:6:
Paul says that he received revelations so extraordinary that he was at risk of becoming conceited. To keep him from that, God allowed "a thorn in my flesh," meaning something that caused him constant pain, like a thorn stuck in the body. He calls it "a messenger of Satan" sent "to torment me," that is, to cause him real suffering.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against teachers who boasted about their achievements. Earlier he described an incredible spiritual experience, but he prefers to speak of his weaknesses. We do not know for certain what the thorn was: some think of an illness, others of opposition or persecution. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God can use our limitations to keep us humble and dependent on Him. When something hurts and does not go away, remember that His grace is enough for you.
exp.10:25:
Paul lists the dangers he faced on his many journeys: rivers he had to cross, bandits along the way, danger from his own countrymen and from the Gentiles, danger in the city and out in the open country, danger at sea, and danger from false brothers, meaning people who claimed to be believers but were not.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his calling as an apostle. Some proud teachers looked down on him. Instead of boasting about his successes, Paul points to the hardships he endured for serving Christ. In effect he is saying: a life given over to God, marked by these sufferings, shows that my service is genuine.

Today, this reminds us that serving God can cost us and is not always comfortable. If you go through hardship for doing what is right, do not assume that God has abandoned you. Keep going with humility and confidence in Him.
exp.7:17:
Paul says that along with Titus he is sending another brother, one who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel. The word "together" in the verse means "at the same time, in company," so the sense is that this brother went along with Titus. The praise is for his work in spreading the good news, which points to a good reputation among the churches for faithful service.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish the gift they had promised for the poor believers in Jerusalem. That is why he sends Titus with two trusted companions. The Bible does not give this brother's name, and various ideas have been suggested since early times, but there is no certainty.

Today we can learn that the handling of money in the church should be done with openness and by people of good reputation. If we serve in something that involves other people's resources, it is wise to work as a team and give a clear account, so that no one has reason for suspicion.
exp.11:17:
Paul says that he urged Titus to visit Corinth, and that he sent another brother along with him. Then he asks questions: Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps? The phrase "follow in the same footsteps" describes the way one lives and conducts oneself, the pattern of one's whole life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against suspicions. Some were saying that he had manipulated them, perhaps through his messengers, to get money from them. His answer is to remind them that Titus and he acted with the same honesty. Interpreters agree that the subject is integrity in handling financial help, although the text gives no further details.

For today: live with transparency, so that our actions and those of the people who work with us can withstand any question. And when someone doubts us, respond with humility, honesty, and clear facts.
exp.1:1:
