He says that if he causes the Corinthians sorrow, who will cheer him up? Only the very people he had grieved. The word "grieve" in the verse means causing sadness or pain. Here, the word "then" means "in that case" or "afterward." Paul shows that his joy and theirs are closely bound together.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a tense and painful relationship. He had to correct them firmly. For that reason he decided not to make another painful visit, but to write to them first, so that the resolving of the problems would allow a joyful visit. Some scholars think he is referring to an earlier letter; others hold different views, and the Bible does not settle the question completely.

For today: when you have to correct someone, do it with love and with their good in mind, not to wound. And remember that in the church and in the family joy is shared, and that a sincere correction can prepare the way for comfort and restoration.
exp.5:4:
In beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger: these are concrete hardships. Beatings are blows that were inflicted on the body. Imprisonments are times when Paul and his companions were locked up. Riots are crowds or disturbances, sometimes violent. Labor is hard work that wears a person out. Sleepless nights are times when they could not rest. Hunger is going without food, whether from lack of provision or by circumstance.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. He wants them to see that he is not a self-interested preacher, but a servant of God. For that reason he presents what he suffered as proof of his sincerity. Some of these hardships appear in other passages, such as 2 Corinthians 11:23-27. The text does not make clear which periods of hunger were chosen and which were forced on them.

Today, this invites us not to measure service to God only by comfort or success. If we face difficulties for doing good, we can continue with patience, trusting that God sustains those who serve him sincerely.
exp.1:12:
Paul says that he had no peace in his spirit because he did not find his brother Titus there. So he said goodbye to the people in Troas and went on to Macedonia.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. He had sent Titus to learn how they had received his earlier letter, and he hoped to meet him in Troas. Although there was an open door there for preaching, his concern for the church in Corinth weighed more heavily. Commentators debate how long he stayed in Troas, but the text does not make this clear.

God is concerned not only with our tasks but also with people and relationships. If something troubles you about someone you love, do not ignore it: pray, seek reconciliation, and take the necessary step.
exp.3:17:
The text says that Christians do not fix their attention on what can be seen, but on what is unseen. The reason is simple: what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Corinth. He tells them that he suffers persecution and exhaustion, but he does not give up. His body wears down, while his inner life is renewed each day. For this reason he looks beyond his present pain, toward the glory that God promises. Many understand that what is unseen includes God's promises and life with Him.

For today: when you are going through a trial, do not stay only looking at the problem. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, remembering that God is still at work and that your hope does not depend on what you see.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that when we receive our heavenly dwelling, we will be found "clothed" and not "naked." Paul uses the image of clothing to speak about the body. Being "naked" suggests being without a body, and being "clothed" refers to having the new body that God gives. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the wording, and some readers take the phrase in a different sense.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He speaks to them of the hope of the resurrection in the midst of suffering and the frailty of present life. He compares the current body to a tent and the future to an eternal house. Interpreters differ on whether he is speaking of an intermediate state after death, but his confidence in God is clear.

Today, when the body grows tired or life hurts, we can rest in the fact that God is preparing something better for us. Let us live with hope, trusting in the Spirit he gave us as a guarantee.
exp.12:4:
The explanation says that the Corinthians should examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith. "Examine" and "test" mean to evaluate honestly. Paul's words "unless you fail the test" describe a faith that does not hold up under honest scrutiny, like a coin that turns out to be counterfeit. Paul reminds them that Jesus Christ is in them, unless they fail the test.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, with whom he had tensions. Some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Paul turns the question back on them: instead of examining him, let them examine themselves. Their changed lives would be evidence of his ministry.

For today: before judging others, take a moment alone with God and ask yourself honestly how your faith, your love, and your obedience are doing. Ask him to show you what you need to correct.
exp.8:5:
What it says: Paul uses the image of sowing seed. Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. "Sparingly" means with a small amount, held back. "Reap" means to harvest what has been planted. "Generously" speaks of giving freely, as a blessing to others.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the gift they had promised for the believers in need in Jerusalem. He sends some brothers ahead so that everything is ready and the gift does not seem to be given grudgingly. Interpreters debate whether the harvest refers to material rewards, spiritual ones, or both. The verses that follow emphasize the grace of God, not a simple exchange.

For today: When you have the chance to help, prepare your help in advance and give with joy, trusting that God cares for the one who gives generously.
exp.5:14:
This verse asks two questions to show that Christ and Belial cannot walk together. "Harmony" means agreement or unity. "Belial" is a name used to speak of wickedness and, here, of Satan. A "believer" is the one who trusts in Christ, and an "unbeliever" is the one who does not. The implied answer is: nothing.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he treats with affection as his children. He asks them not to be bound unevenly with unbelievers, like two animals yoked together under a shared burden that pulls in different directions. Interpreters debate whether he means mainly idolatry, marriage, or partnerships in general, and perhaps all of these.

Today, before we commit to a partnership, a relationship, or a cause, let us ask whether we will be able to remain faithful to Christ. That does not mean looking down on anyone: we still love and serve everyone.
exp.5:15:
Paul asks what agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols. The answer is: none. He affirms that believers are the temple of the living God, quoting Old Testament promises where God says he will dwell with his people and walk among them, and that he will be their God and they will be his people.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church surrounded by temples and idol worship. He urges them not to be bound together, like animals under the same yoke, with those who do not believe. Scholars discuss whether he is speaking of marriage, business, or taking part in pagan worship; the text shows the general idea of not sharing loyalties.

For today: if God lives in you, be careful about what enters your life. Examine which friendships, commitments, or habits compete with your faith, and ask God for wisdom to live faithfully without despising anyone.
exp.11:9:
Paul says that he delights in his weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, and in difficulties, as long as they come for the sake of Christ. In this verse, "weak" means lacking strength, and "strong" means having power. His point is that when he admits his weakness, God's power works in him.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending his authority as an apostle against others who boasted of their achievements. Just before this, he tells how he asked three times for God to take away a suffering that he calls a thorn in the flesh, and the Lord answered him: "My grace is sufficient for you." Scholars do not know for certain what that thorn was.

Today, when you feel limited or tired, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you lack and ask him to sustain you by his grace. His help comes right in those moments.
exp.3:3:
There is a spiritual power, called "the god of this age," that has blinded the minds of unbelievers. The phrase "of this age" refers to the present world and its way of thinking. Because of that blindness, unbelievers cannot see the light of the gospel, which shows the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. Many understand that this "god" is Satan, although he is not a true God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry. He preaches with honesty, without deception. If someone does not understand the message, it is not because it is poorly explained, but because there is a spiritual blindness. Then he makes clear that he does not preach himself, but Jesus Christ as Lord.

Today we can pray for those who do not believe, instead of arguing with them or judging them. We present Christ with sincerity and trust that only God opens the eyes of the heart.
exp.10:7:
Paul says that he "robbed" other churches, meaning that he acted like someone who takes what does not belong to him. By this he means that those churches supported him with their gifts while he was serving the Corinthians. The word "serve" in the verse means to minister to them, and "in order to" points to the purpose of that support.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth where some people criticized him and favored other teachers who charged fees. He uses strong, almost ironic language to defend the fact that he preached to them without cost. Scholars understand his words as deliberate exaggeration, not as an actual theft.

Today we can support generously those who serve in the church and in missions. And those who serve can do so with humility, without seeking their own benefit, thinking of the good of others.
exp.0:5:
Paul says that his sufferings have a purpose that benefits the Corinthians. If he goes through affliction, it is for their comfort and salvation. If he is comforted, that too is for their comfort. "Salvation" here means being saved, which includes spiritual well-being. The comfort he receives works in them, and it shows when they patiently endure the same sufferings he experiences.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had had a strained relationship. He explains to them that his suffering as an apostle is not a sign that God has abandoned him. Shortly afterward he recounts a very hard trial he experienced in Asia. He wants them to understand that they are united in suffering and in comfort.

For today: when God comforts you in a difficulty, do not keep that comfort only for yourself. Think of someone who is suffering something similar and offer them your company, a phone call, or a prayer.
exp.7:9:
In this verse Paul says he is giving his opinion, not a command, about the offering for the struggling believers. It is good for the Corinthians to finish what they began. Last year they were the first, not only to give, but even to have the desire to give. "It is good for you" means it does them good, and "to have such a desire" refers to the wish to give in the first place.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They had promised to help the believers in Jerusalem who were struggling, but the project had lost its momentum. Paul does not press them with authority. He reminds them of the example of Christ, who became poor out of love for them, and he invites them to respond with sincerity.

For today: think of something good you promised or wanted to do, such as helping someone or supporting a need, that was left half finished. Take one concrete step today to complete it, with joy and according to what you have.
exp.10:12:
Paul says that some people who present themselves as apostles are actually false ones. They are deceitful workers who cheat people. "Masquerading as apostles" means they put on the appearance of genuine apostles of Christ when they are not.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he founded. Teachers had come there who praised themselves and questioned his authority. Paul makes clear that his love for them is real and that he will not change his conduct, so that those teachers have no reason to boast. Right after this he says that Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

For today: do not be impressed only by appearance, charisma, or a leader's titles. Always compare what they teach with the Bible, and look at whether their life reflects the character of Christ.
exp.10:17:
Paul says that since many people boast about human things, such as achievements, family background, and prestige, he will boast too. To "boast" means to brag or take pride in something. "Foolish" here means senseless or without good judgment.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, the church he founded. Some teachers who presented themselves as superior were winning them over and attacking Paul. He does not like boasting and warns that he is not speaking the way the Lord would have him speak, but with irony, like a fool. He does this so that they will see the emptiness of that kind of pride. Shortly afterward, he will boast of his weaknesses and sufferings.

For today: do not be impressed by someone who boasts of titles, success, or appearance. Measure people by their character and their faithfulness to Christ. And examine your own heart: what do you boast in?
exp.3:7:
It says that Paul and his companions go through many trials, but they are not crushed. The words "hard pressed" and "crushed" in the verse describe feeling squeezed by hardship, and "perplexed" means being without resources or not knowing what to do. "Despair" means losing all hope. So they suffer, but there is always a way out and a hope.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth and speaking about his ministry. He has just said that they carry the treasure of the gospel in fragile vessels, that is, in fragile people. This shows that the strength comes from God and not from them. These opposing phrases express that idea: they are weak, but God sustains them.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, you do not have to pretend that it does not hurt. Be honest with God about your weariness and your doubts, and trust that his power sustains you even when your own strength runs out. Also ask for the support of your Christian community.
exp.11:2:
Paul says again that he knows a person who had an extraordinary experience. He does not know whether it happened in the body or outside of it, but God knows. "This man" refers to a man like the one he is describing. The word "whether" introduces the two possibilities he is weighing.

Paul speaks indirectly, as if he were talking about someone else, though many readers understand that he is really speaking of himself. He is defending his standing before some Corinthians who doubted his authority. He does not want to boast, so he speaks of his visions and revelations with care and humility. His real source of pride, he says, lies in his weaknesses.

For today: we do not need to understand everything to trust God. Paul simply admits that there are things he does not know. We can do the same, leave what we do not understand in God's hands, and avoid using our spiritual experiences to feel superior.
exp.12:13:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. Here "fellowship" means a shared partnership. Paul wishes that believers would live out the undeserved kindness of Christ, the love of the Father, and the unity that the Spirit gives.

Paul closes his second letter to the Corinthians, a church marked by many tensions and much pain. He writes to them with affection, but also with firmness, and ends with a blessing that names the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. Many see here one of the clearest expressions of the Trinity in the New Testament, although the word itself does not appear.

For today: when you say goodbye to someone, try to bless them sincerely, asking God to give them grace, love, and fellowship, and not just a "take care."
exp.9:10:
Paul says that the person who criticizes him should consider this: what he is in his letters when he is far away, he will also be in his actions when he is present. "Such people" are the ones who are judging him. "Letters" refers to what he writes, and "actions" to what he does.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some were accusing him of being bold only on paper, but weak and unimpressive in person. He answers that there is no difference between his written message and his actual conduct. He wants to correct them with authority given by God, but he prefers that it not be necessary to do so harshly.

For today: let us seek to make our words and our lives agree. May we be the same people in public and in private, in messages and in person. Integrity gives weight to what we say.
exp.7:20:
Paul says that he and his companions take great care to do what is good and right, not only because God sees them, but also because people are watching them. "What is right" here means what is good, honorable, and clean. "Taking great care" means working carefully and intentionally to look after something.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth about the money being gathered to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. The churches had chosen a brother to travel with Paul and handle the money. That way, no one could suspect him or accuse him of mishandling it.

If you handle money or responsibilities in the church or at work, do it with clarity and order. Keep records, report honestly, and let others help review. In this way you guard your witness and honor God.
exp.2:1:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they are the letter that recommends him and his companions. That letter is not written on paper but inscribed on Paul's heart. The word "letter" means a written message, and "known and read by everyone" means that everyone can recognize it and read it.

Paul writes to a church that he himself founded in Corinth. Some were carrying letters of recommendation to gain acceptance, and others were questioning Paul's authority. He answers that he does not need that kind of paper: the changed lives of the Corinthian believers are the proof that his ministry is genuine.

For today: our lives are what people read most about Christ. You might ask yourself: what does the way I treat others say about Jesus? Ask the Spirit to help you live in such a way that others see his work in you.
exp.7:2:
Paul says that the churches of Macedonia gave of their own accord, meaning by their own willingness, with no one forcing them. He says they gave according to their ability, and even beyond it, more than seemed possible. Paul adds, "I testify," as a direct witness to what he saw.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians about the collection for believers in need, probably those in Jerusalem. He holds up the Macedonians as an example; they lived in affliction and poverty, yet they gave with joy. He does not do this to pressure them, but to encourage Corinth to complete its own help.

For today: Christian generosity springs from a grateful and free heart, not from obligation. Ask yourself what you can give with joy, whether money, time, or help, even if your situation is limited.
exp.10:4:
Paul says that he considers himself in no way inferior to those "super-apostles." The phrase "in no way" means "not at all" or "not in the least," so his point is that he counted himself equal to them. He does not speak with empty pride, but defends his calling.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who are worried that teachers will come preaching "another Jesus" and another gospel. Some of them boasted of their authority and eloquence, and looked down on Paul. He calls them "super-apostles" with a certain irony; scholars debate whether he means the leaders in Jerusalem or those deceptive teachers. Many think he means the latter, though this is not entirely certain.

Today, let us not measure a teacher by his fame or his fine speaking, but by whether he faithfully preaches Jesus and the gospel we receive in the Bible.
exp.3:16:
This verse compares two things: our present sufferings and the glory that is coming. Paul says that the affliction is "light" and "momentary," lasting only a short time, while the glory is an "eternal weight" that is far beyond comparison. The word "producing" means that the affliction is bringing about or preparing us for that glory.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom he had served in the midst of persecutions, weariness, and dangers. He does not deny that he suffers; in other passages of the letter he describes his pains in detail. But he looks at his suffering in the light of eternity and of the inner renewal that God gives him each day. Some understand that suffering "produces" the glory; others understand that it prepares for it under God's grace.

Today, when you are going through a difficulty, do not minimize it, but do not let it be the only thing you see. Ask God to renew your spirit today, and remember that your pain is not the last word.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that it is God who keeps both us and you firm together in Christ, and that it is he who anointed us. "Establishes" means to make firm and secure. "Anointed" means to set someone apart for God and give them a task, as oil was used for this purpose in biblical times.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. Some doubted him because he had changed his travel plans, and they saw him as someone who said "yes" and "no" at the same time. Paul answers that his message is trustworthy because it comes from God, who fulfills what he promises in Christ. His steadfastness does not depend on himself, but on God.

For today: when you feel unsure of your faith or your calling, remember that God is the one who sustains you. Rest in his faithfulness, and ask him to make you firm and trustworthy in what you say and do.
exp.3:9:
Paul says that he and his companions always carry the death of Jesus in their own bodies. In other words, they bear sufferings like those Jesus himself endured. But this has a purpose: that the life of Jesus, his power and his strength, may also be revealed in those same fragile bodies. To "reveal" here means to show, to make visible.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about the hardships he faces while preaching the good news. The verses just before this one show the contrast: he is struck down, but he is not destroyed. He says that we are like clay jars, fragile, so that the power may be seen as coming from God and not from us. Some understand the "death" as real persecution; others understand it as a life of daily self-giving.

For today: when you are tired, limited, or going through a trial, do not hide it or become discouraged. Ask God that, in the middle of your weakness, others may see his strength and his hope in you.
exp.5:2:
Paul and his companions take care not to put any obstacle in anyone's way. The word "obstacle" here means something that makes others stumble or turns them away from the faith. The word "discredit" means criticize or speak ill of. So the purpose is that their conduct not undermine the work of proclaiming the good news.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a difficult relationship. He has just urged them not to receive the grace of God in vain, for now is the time of salvation. As a messenger of Christ, he knows that his way of living can either help or hinder the message. For this reason, in the verses that follow, he describes how he has remained faithful even in suffering.

For today: before you speak or act, ask yourself whether your conduct helps others see Christ or pushes them away. Guard your honesty, your treatment of others, and your words, not seeking applause but honoring God.
exp.5:5:
This verse continues a list of qualities that show how a true servant of God lives. "Purity" means a clean and upright way of living. "Knowledge" is spiritual understanding. "Patience" is staying steady with people, enduring without giving up. "Kindness" is gentle and generous treatment of others. The verse also mentions the Holy Spirit and a love that is sincere, free of pretense.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted his authority. For that reason he presents no credentials, but rather his conduct: hardships, purity, and love. There are different opinions about whether "in the Holy Spirit" refers to the Spirit of God working in him or to a holy spirit, but most understand it as the Spirit of God.

For today: ask yourself whether your love is sincere. This week, serve someone without expecting recognition or applause, and treat them with real patience and kindness.
exp.10:3:
Paul says that if someone comes proclaiming a Jesus other than the one he proclaimed to them, or if they receive a different spirit than the one they received, or a different gospel than the one they accepted, they put up with it very easily. "Put up with" means to endure or tolerate. It is a rebuke: the Corinthians accept readily what they should not.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself founded. He feels a holy jealousy for them, like a father protecting his daughter before her wedding. He fears they will be deceived, as Eve was, and drift away from the simplicity that is in Christ. Some teachers presented themselves as superior to him, and that is why he mentions "those super-apostles." Interpreters debate exactly who they were.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Jesus says in the Bible. If it presents a different Christ or a message that changes the gospel, do not accept it just because it sounds attractive.
exp.4:5:
What it says: Paul states that believers live with courage and confidence, even though they know that while they are in this earthly body, they are away from the Lord. The explanation's word for "traveling" means walking like travelers in a foreign land, on the way to our true home. Being "confident" means having good courage without losing heart.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, speaking of hardships and of the fragile body, which he calls a temporary tent. His courage comes from the fact that God has already given them the Spirit as a guarantee of what is to come. The following verses explain that we walk by faith and not by sight.

For today: When you feel tiredness, pain, or doubt, remember that this life is not the end. Take a few minutes today to thank God for his promise, and ask him that his Spirit give you confidence to keep going with hope.
exp.6:13:
Paul says that he had spoken well of the Corinthians to Titus, and that he was not embarrassed by it. The word "boasting" in this verse means that he took pride in them and spoke with confidence about them. The phrase "has proved to be true" means that what he said turned out to be correct, just as everything else he had told them had.

Paul writes to a church with which he had experienced tension. Titus had visited Corinth and came back encouraged by how they welcomed him. Paul rejoices because his confidence in them was not misplaced. Scholars debate exactly which offense the context refers to, but the general tone is one of relief and closeness.

Today, we can speak well of others and trust the best in them. We can also live in such a way that those who believed in us have no reason to be embarrassed. A kind word and sincere confidence encourage many.
exp.7:19:
The explanation says that Paul and his team want to prevent anyone from criticizing them or speaking badly of them for the way they handle this generous gift. The word "criticism" in the verse above is the word the explanation is describing: it means to find fault with, or to accuse harshly. "The way we administer this generous gift" refers to the large amount of money they are managing and carrying.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish their gift for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. Since it involves a great deal of money, he takes care that everything is done in an orderly way and that others accompany and oversee the handling of it. In this way no one can suspect him.

For today: if you handle money belonging to the church or to other people, do everything with transparency and as a team. Being accountable is not distrust; it is a way of protecting the witness and the trust of everyone.
exp.10:16:
Paul says that what he is about to say now, that is, his boasting, he does not say as the Lord would have him say it, but as a fool would. It means: he is speaking the way a fool would speak. The "confident boasting" refers to the confidence with which he sets himself to talk about himself.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he founded in the faith. Some "super apostles" had won them over with their credentials and showy claims, and they were discrediting Paul. He dislikes boasting, but he feels compelled to do it, as in a game of fools, to show that his accusers are not superior. Scholars debate how much of this is irony, but the tone is clear: he does it with reluctance.

For today: boasting about our achievements is not the way of the Lord. If we ever must defend our name or service, let us do it with humility, brevity, and without losing sight of the fact that all true glory belongs to Christ.
exp.11:10:
Paul says he has acted like a fool by boasting about himself, but he insists the Corinthians drove him to it. The word "drove" means they pushed him into it, and "super-apostles" refers to those supposedly superior apostles. He claims he was in no way inferior to them, though he admits that in himself he is "nothing."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some arrogant teachers criticized him and questioned his authority. The Corinthians should have defended him, but they did not. That is why he boasts reluctantly, with a certain irony. Scholars debate who these "super-apostles" were: the apostles in Jerusalem, or the false teachers who passed themselves off as them.

For today: when you have to defend your calling or your work, do it with humility and without pride. Remember that whatever is valuable in you comes from the grace of God, not from your own merits.
exp.8:7:
This verse says that God is able to make all grace abound toward you, that is, his favor and his blessings. So that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work. The phrase "so that" introduces the purpose of God's grace, and "having all that you need" refers to having enough of everything required.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth to encourage them to take part in the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God loves the one who gives with joy, and that God is the one who provides what is needed so that they can give generously.

For today: when you have the opportunity to help someone, do not think only about what you lack. Trust that God can supply what you need, and give with joy, knowing that your generosity is a good work that he himself supports.
exp.4:9:
It says that all of us, without exception, will have to appear before the judgment seat of Christ. The verse's "must" is the word for what is necessary, and the verse's "appear" means that we must present ourselves there. There each person will receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad. Christians understand this moment in different ways, but the text speaks of a real accounting.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. He had just been talking about his desire to be with the Lord and to please him, whether in this life or the next. He was also defending the sincerity of his ministry against those who criticized him and looked only at outward appearances.

For today: live each day with the awareness that Christ sees your motives, not just your appearances. Before deciding something, ask yourself: "Is this pleasing to the Lord?" Do it with confidence and reverence, not with fear.
exp.11:5:
Paul says that even if he wanted to boast, he would not be a fool, because he would be telling the truth. But he holds back. "Fool" means someone who lacks sense, and "boast" here means to brag about oneself. He does not want anyone to credit him with more than they can see in his life or hear from his own words.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who bragged about visions and power. He had mentioned an extraordinary experience from about fourteen years earlier, and now he stops. He would rather be judged by how he lives and what he says, not by experiences that no one can check. Right after this, he speaks of his weakness.

For today: you do not need to impress others with your achievements or spiritual experiences. Let your life and your words speak for you, with humility and honesty.
exp.10:6:
Paul asks a question with a touch of irony: Was it a sin for me to humble myself so that you could be raised up, because I preached the good news of God to you free of charge? "Raised up" means lifted into a better condition, or enriched spiritually. "Free of charge" means without asking for any payment.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his authority against certain "super apostles" who were criticizing him. He did not charge them, working with his own hands and receiving help from other churches. Some in Corinth seem to have seen this as a sign of weakness. Paul shows them that his sacrifice came from love and not from a lack of worth.

For today: let us not measure the value of a service by its shine or its price, but by the love with which it is done. And when someone serves with humility, let us thank them instead of looking down on them.
exp.7:10:
Paul asks the Corinthians to finish what they started. "Finish the work" means to complete the task. They had a good desire and were eager to help. Now they should show that same eagerness in following through, giving according to what they have, that is, according to their means.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had begun the collection the year before, but it seems it had stalled. Paul encourages them by reminding them of the example of Christ, who, though rich, became poor for their sake.

For today: if God has placed in your heart the desire to help someone or to serve in some way, do not let it remain a good intention. Take a concrete step this week with what you really have, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.4:8:
Because of what comes before, Paul and his companions aim to please God. The verse uses the word "aspire," which means they direct real effort and desire toward this goal. Their aim stays the same whether they are still at home in this body or away from it. In other words, whether they are alive in the body or already with the Lord, their goal is to please him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about the hope of being with the Lord after death. Even so, he does not let that hope make him passive. Next he mentions that all of us will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Some understand this as an evaluation of the Christian life, not as a condemnation. Paul also defends the sincerity of his ministry.

For today: make pleasing God your daily aim, not only at church but at work, at home, and in small decisions, trusting in his grace and not acting out of fear.
exp.0:10:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they are helping him too, by praying for him. The "favor" is the kindness of God, which here means God rescuing him from a deadly danger. The phrase "as you help us by your prayers" shows that this favor came in answer to the prayers of many people. The result is that many will give thanks to God on his behalf.

Paul writes from a time of great distress, which he describes in the verses before, when he felt he was going to die. It is not known for certain exactly what it was, and scholars understand it in several ways. He confesses that he learned to rely only on God, who raises the dead, and he asks the church to keep praying.

For today: our prayer for others truly matters. This week you can pray for a pastor, a missionary, or a friend in trouble, and then rejoice and give thanks to God when he answers.
exp.2:5:
God himself has qualified Paul and his companions to serve as ministers of a new covenant. The word translated "qualified" means made capable or fit for the task. This covenant is not based on the written law treated only as outside rules, but on the Spirit. The letter kills because it exposes sin and brings condemnation but gives no power to change; the Spirit gives life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some questioned his authority. He does not boast in his own strength, but says that his ability comes from God. He then compares the ministry of Moses, written on stone, with the ministry of the Spirit, which is more glorious. Some interpreters debate the details of what "letter" and "spirit" mean, but the general contrast is clear.

Today, do not live your faith only as a list of duties. Ask the Holy Spirit to transform your heart, and trust that God equips you for what he entrusts to you.
exp.10:10:
Paul asks the Corinthians: "Why? Is it because I do not love you?" And he answers right away: "God knows I do!" He puts God forward as the witness of his heart.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was being influenced by false apostles. Paul had preached among them without charging them, and some may have read that as a lack of affection or of authority. He explains that he will keep doing this in order to deny those deceptive teachers the chance to boast that they are equal to him. His motives were love and purity of intention, not coldness.

For today: love does not always show itself the way others expect. When someone misreads your good intentions, don't defend yourself with anger. Place them before God, keep serving with integrity, and let time reveal your heart.
exp.9:13:
Paul says that he is not going beyond the limits God gave him. He does not boast beyond what is right, as though his work had never reached Corinth. The phrase "overstepping our bounds" means boasting or acting outside the field that was assigned. He affirms that he did reach them, because he was the first to bring them the gospel of Christ.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had been influenced by other teachers who praised themselves and questioned his authority. He answers with firmness but without arrogance: his authority does not come from comparing himself with others, but from the work God entrusted to him. Corinth was part of that work.

For today: serve where God has placed you, without comparing yourself with others or boasting of what you did not do. Be thankful for your place, do well what was entrusted to you, and let God be the one who gives you worth.
exp.11:7:
Paul says that he pleaded with the Lord three times to take away the thorn, the suffering that troubled him. The phrase "take it away from me" means that it would be removed from his life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against those who boasted of their achievements. He speaks of his revelations and of a thorn in his flesh that kept him humble. It is not known for certain what it was: some think of an illness, others of opposition or persecution. The text does not make it clear. Christ did not remove it, but answered him: "My grace is sufficient for you."

Today we can pray sincerely and persistently about what hurts us. If God does not take it away, that does not mean he has abandoned us. His grace sustains us, and his power can be shown in our weakness.
exp.1:15:
The explanation says that the message of Christ, which Paul and his companions proclaim, is received in two ways. For those who reject it, it is like an odor that brings death; for those who welcome it, it is a fragrance that brings life. Then Paul asks: "who is qualified for such a task?", that is, who is fit for a responsibility this serious?

Paul writes to the Corinthians and speaks about his ministry. He uses the image of a victorious parade, where incense fills the air everywhere. Some understand this as a reference to Roman parades, though not everyone agrees. In the following verse, he answers that he does not preach for gain, but with sincerity before God.

For today: when you share your faith, do not depend on your own ability. Speak with honesty and trust that God is the one who opens hearts, even though some respond well and others do not.
exp.7:15:
He says that Paul thanks God because God placed into Titus's heart the same devotion Paul has for the Corinthians. The word "devotion" here describes a deep, committed care, a real desire to serve them well.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish their offering for the poor Christians in Judea. He had already spoken about generosity and about fairness between the churches. Now he introduces Titus, who would carry this letter and help complete the collection. Paul recognizes that this care for them comes from God.

For today: when you see someone serving with love and dedication, thank God for that person. And ask him to also give you a heart attentive to the needs of others, so that you help with sincerity and not only out of obligation.
exp.9:3:
It says that Paul and his companions are fighting a battle, but not with the weapons of the flesh. The word "warfare" here means the struggle or service of a soldier, and the weapons are not human weapons or the methods of this world. Their weapons have divine power and can demolish strongholds, that is, deeply rooted ideas and attitudes that resist the truth.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because some were accusing him of acting out of human interests. He admits that he lives in a weak body, but makes clear that his ministry does not depend on tricks or on his own strength. The verses that follow speak of pulling down arguments and bringing every thought into obedience to Christ.

For today: when you face a conflict or a lie that seems impossible to overcome, do not respond with pride or anger. Pray, use the truth of the Bible, and act with love and patience, trusting that God is at work.
exp.0:6:
Paul says that his hope for the Corinthians is sure, meaning it does not waver. He is confident that just as they share in the sufferings, they will also share in the comfort that comes from God. "Partners" means companions or participants, people who go together through both the good and the hard times.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom he had experienced tensions. He speaks to them of his own afflictions and of the comfort he received from God. Soon he will tell them about a very harsh trial he went through in Asia, where he felt he would die. He wants them to know that suffering and comfort go together.

Today, if you are going through a trial because you follow Christ, you are not alone. God comforts you, and that comfort is not only for you: you can share it with others who suffer, accompanying them with prayer, listening, and words of encouragement.
exp.2:13:
It says that the minds of many Israelites were closed. They could not grasp what they were reading. Even today, when the old covenant is read, a veil still covers its meaning. Paul affirms that this veil cannot be lifted by effort or study alone, but only in Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and compares his ministry with that of Moses, who covered his face when he came down from the mountain. Paul speaks of his own countrymen, who read the law without recognizing Christ in it. Some understand the fading glory in this passage as the close of the old covenant, and others interpret it in other ways.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to open your understanding and look for Christ on every page. He gives light to those who come near with humility.
exp.11:8:
Paul tells what the Lord answered when he asked three times that his thorn be taken away: "My grace is sufficient for you," that is, his undeserved favor and help. God's power is brought to completion in weakness, meaning that it is shown at its fullest when human strength runs out. That is why Paul gladly boasts in his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted his authority and admired other teachers who seemed more impressive. He speaks of an extraordinary revelation and of a "thorn in the flesh." We do not know for certain what it was; a sickness, an opposition, or a personal trial have been suggested, but the text does not say.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. Bring your weariness or your limits to God honestly, and trust that his grace sustains you right there.
exp.6:8:
Paul says that he now rejoices, but not because the Corinthians were made to feel sorrow. He rejoices because their sorrow led them to repentance and a change of direction. The word "sorrow" here refers to being grieved or deeply pained. It was the sorrow that God intended, the kind that works toward something good. In this way they were not harmed by anything Paul did.

Paul had written them a firm letter to correct them, and that caused them pain. Later Titus brought him good news: the church had responded with seriousness and a real desire to change their ways. That is why Paul writes to them with relief. He makes clear that his joy is not in having hurt them, but in the good fruit that came afterward.

For today: when someone corrects you with love, do not become defensive right away. Ask yourself before God whether there is something you need to change. The sorrow that leads you back to God brings healing; it does not destroy.
exp.3:15:
Paul and his companions say that they do not give up or lose heart. "Not losing heart" means not becoming discouraged or surrendering. Our outer self is our physical life, the body, which is wasting away, that is, it grows weaker through suffering and the passing of time. Our inner self is the life of the spirit, which is being renewed day by day: God strengthens it each day.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth and speaks of the hardships he endures while preaching the gospel. He has just said that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise them. For this reason he sees his trials as something temporary, compared with the eternal glory he mentions next.

For today: when tiredness, illness, or problems wear you down, do not lose heart. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, so that God renews your inner strength and reminds you of the hope that cannot be seen.
exp.11:0:
Paul says that boasting is neither helpful nor fitting for him. Even so, he is going to speak of "visions" and "revelations," that is, experiences in which the Lord showed him things in a supernatural way. Here, the wording "I must go on boasting" shows that he feels he has no choice, and the phrase "Although there is nothing to gain" shows that he does not expect any benefit from it.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted his authority because some "super-apostles" bragged about their achievements. To defend himself, Paul feels compelled to speak about himself, but he does so reluctantly. In the verses that follow he speaks of a man in Christ, and many understand this to refer to himself, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: if God is at work in your life, give thanks and speak of Him with humility. Do not use your spiritual experiences to feel superior, but to encourage others.
exp.9:9:
This verse repeats what some people were saying about Paul: his letters are serious and forceful, but when he is in person he seems unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some critics questioned his authority. He insists that the power God gave him is meant to build up, not to tear down. In the verses that follow, he makes clear that he is the same whether writing from a distance or present in person. Some scholars think his critics judged by appearance and eloquence.

For today: let us not measure people by their presence or by the way they speak. And if someone criticizes us, we can respond with consistency, being the same in what we say and in what we do.
exp.11:15:
Paul says he admits he was not a burden to the Corinthians in money matters. Then, with irony, he repeats what some were saying: that, though crafty as he was, he had caught them by trickery. The words "crafty" and "caught by trickery" are the accusation his critics were making, not a compliment. To be a burden means to be weighed down or loaded with a cost. To catch someone by trickery means to trap them through a deceptive scheme.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against critics who doubted his honesty. Although he had not charged them anything, someone was suggesting that he had a hidden plan to profit from them. That is why, in the verses that follow, he mentions Titus and the brothers sent with him, and asks whether any of them took advantage of the church. His open life was his answer.

When someone serves with generosity, others sometimes doubt his motives. We can respond without anger, with openness and a good witness. And if we serve, let us examine our hearts to seek people, not their benefits.
exp.1:3:
Paul says he wrote a very firm letter, but he did it with great pain and in tears. "Great distress" and "anguish of heart" speak of a deep sorrow. "Grieve" means to sadden. His purpose was not to hurt them, but to let them know how much he loves them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a conflict with them. He had sent them a firm letter to correct a serious matter. Many scholars think that letter is different from 1 Corinthians, though there is no complete certainty. Now he wants them to understand that his correction came from love, and he desires to come back to them with joy, not with more sadness.

For today: when you need to correct someone, do it with truth, but also with tenderness and a sincere desire for their good. And when someone corrects you in love, try to see their heart behind the hard words.
exp.12:8:
He says that Paul is glad when he is weak and the Corinthians are strong in the faith. Here "perfection" speaks of maturity and being made whole, not of having no flaws. Paul's prayer is that the church grow and be complete in its Christian life.

The apostle Paul writes to a church with conflicts, where some questioned his authority. Before visiting them, he invites them to examine themselves and to correct what is wrong. He does not seek to look good or to show his power. If they walk in the truth, he will not have to use his authority in a harsh way, and he does not mind appearing weak.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are glad to see others grow, even when we receive no recognition. A good leader, parent, teacher, or friend serves so that others become stronger, without needing to feel superior.
exp.9:17:
It says that speaking well of oneself is not enough to be accepted. What truly counts is the commendation of the Lord. "Commend" here means to speak well of someone or to recommend them, and "approved" means that someone has passed the test and is recognized as genuine.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some teachers were commending themselves and criticizing Paul. He answers that he does not compare himself with others or claim credit for other people's work. His service was to bring the gospel to new places, and if anyone wants to boast, let them boast in the Lord.

For today: before seeking applause or trying to impress others, ask yourself whether what you do pleases God. Serve with sincerity, recognize that every good fruit comes from Him, and let the Lord be the one who gives the final recognition.
exp.7:11:
The verse says that when someone has an eagerness to give, the gift is acceptable according to what that person has, and not according to what they do not have. Eagerness means a heart that is ready and glad to give, and "acceptable" means pleasing and well received.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had begun to gather a gift to help the believers in Jerusalem who were in need. About a year had passed, and Paul encourages them to finish what they started. He makes clear that he is not asking for more than is possible, but that they should give according to what they have.

For today: do not compare yourself or become discouraged by how little you can give. Give with joy what you have, whether time, help, or money, and keep the promise you have made.
exp.8:14:
Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift! It says we give thanks to God for a gift so great that it cannot be fully put into words. "Gift" simply means a gift, and "indescribable" means it cannot be completely expressed or explained. The verse does not spell out here what that gift is, so some think it is Christ himself, others the grace of God in general, and others the unity among believers.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth as he encourages them to give an offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. In the verses before, he explains that this generosity leads others to praise God. With this phrase he closes the topic, reminding them that all human generosity springs from what God has already given first.

For today: before you give your time, your money, or your help, stop to thank God for what you have received. A grateful life becomes generous with more joy.
exp.4:3:
Paul says that while we live in this body, which he calls a "tent" (something temporary and fragile), we feel its weight and we groan. We do not want to be found "unclothed," that is, without a body, but to be "clothed," with a new body placed over the present one. In this way, what is mortal would be "swallowed up" by life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth and speaks of his own sufferings and weaknesses. He compares the present body to a fragile tent and the future body to a heavenly dwelling. God himself prepared us for this and gave us the Spirit as a guarantee. Christians interpret in different ways what happens just after death, but the final hope is clear.

For today: when tiredness, sickness or pain weigh on you, do not lose heart. Your hope is not merely to endure, but the full life God has promised. Ask the Spirit to remind you of that promise every day.
exp.10:8:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that when he was with them and in need, he was not a burden to anyone. The brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what he lacked. Paul is speaking here about not being a trouble or a financial weight to others. He was careful about this then, and he says he will continue to be.

Paul writes to a church where some people questioned his authority, and other teachers presented themselves as superior. He explains that he preached the gospel without asking them for support, so that they would have no reason to criticize him. When he speaks of receiving help from other churches, he is pointing out that other believers supported him while he served in Corinth.

Today we can serve others generously and take care that our decisions do not hinder the gospel. Sometimes it is good to give up a legitimate right out of love, but always with wisdom and without boasting.
exp.10:30:
Paul says that God himself, the Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that what he is saying is true. It is like calling God as a witness. "Forever worthy of praise" means deserving to be praised eternally. "I am not lying" means that he does not exaggerate or make anything up.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against some teachers who boasted of their achievements. He, however, chooses to speak of his weaknesses and sufferings. Since what he is saying is hard to believe, he solemnly affirms that he is telling the truth, and right away he recounts his escape from Damascus in a basket.

For today: let us speak with honesty, without embellishing the story to impress. Living as someone who knows that God sees everything helps us to be sincere, even when we admit our weaknesses.
exp.3:2:
Paul says that if someone does not understand the gospel he preaches, it is because it is veiled from them, as if covered by a curtain. Veiled here means covered or concealed. The words "those who are perishing" refer to people who are walking on a path far from God and have not yet believed.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and defends the honesty of his ministry. He says he does not deceive or change the message. Even so, some do not accept it. He explains that the problem does not lie in the message, and the following verse speaks of a spiritual blindness that keeps people from seeing the light of Christ.

For today: when you share your faith, be honest and clear, without manipulating anyone. If someone does not understand, do not become discouraged or feel guilty. Pray for that person, because only God can open the eyes of the heart.
exp.5:8:
They appear one way to people, but the reality is different. They seem "unknown," yet God knows them well. They seem "dying," yet they are still alive. To be "punished" means to be disciplined or struck with suffering, but not destroyed.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to defend his ministry. Some were criticizing him and doubting him. He shows them that, although he goes through trials, dishonor and dangers, his service is genuine. This list of contrasts is part of that defense, and many scholars see it as an example of how God sustains his servants in the midst of suffering.

For today: if you feel unnoticed, exhausted or undervalued for serving God, remember that He sees you and sustains you. Your worth does not depend on the opinion of people, but on the fact that God knows you.
exp.5:12:
Paul asks the Corinthians to answer his affection in kind. He says he is speaking to them as his own children and urges them: "open wide your hearts also," that is, make room for affection, without closing yourselves off or keeping your distance.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had tensions. He reminds them that he has spoken to them openly and that his heart is open toward them. In his view, the coldness does not come from his side, but from theirs. After this appeal, he goes on to warn them about partnerships with unbelievers, and some understand that the two themes are related: opening the heart to fellow believers and separating from what harms the faith.

For today: if there is a brother or sister in the faith from whom you have drifted apart through pride or hurt, take a concrete step, such as a phone call or an honest conversation, to open your heart to them again.
exp.0:14:
Paul says that, trusting the Corinthians understood his heart and knew he was sincere, he planned to visit them first. He wanted them to receive a double blessing, a second kindness added to the first. The verse's wording is "a double blessing," and that is the idea the reader should hold onto. The word "planned" means "had the intention of."

Paul writes to a church with which he had tensions. Some criticized him because he had changed his travel plans and said that he could not be trusted. Here he begins to explain that his plans came from affection for them, not from whim or deceit. The exact details of that visit are not fully known.

For today: when you have to change a commitment, explain your reasons with humility and honesty. Seek to bless others, and do not let a misunderstanding cool your relationships.
exp.0:22:
Paul says that God is his witness, and he says it with great seriousness, calling on God as a witness to the truth of what he is saying. He affirms that it was in order to spare them that he did not return to Corinth. To spare them here means he wanted to be patient with them and avoid a painful visit. Calling God as witness is like saying: "God knows that I am telling the truth."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some were accusing him of being unreliable or of not taking them seriously. He explains that it was not out of carelessness. He preferred to wait so as not to arrive with harsh rebukes, and so give them time to correct themselves. The verses that follow make clear that he does not seek to dominate their faith, but to help their joy.

For today: when you have to correct someone, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love and patience. Sometimes waiting and speaking calmly serves better than reacting immediately. And if you are misunderstood, explain your motives with humility and sincerity.
exp.4:17:
It says that all the new things Paul has just described come from God. He reconciled us to himself through Christ, that is, he brought us near to himself and ended the hostility. He also gave us a task: to announce that reconciliation.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, a church under strain, where some questioned his authority. He has just spoken of the new creation, and here he explains that this change is not a human achievement. He also maintains that his ministry comes from God, not from himself.

For today: if God brought you near to himself without your having earned it, you can live with gratitude instead of fear. And you can share that good news with humility, inviting others to be reconciled to God, just as you were welcomed.

sum.10: Paul defends his ministry to the Corinthians because he is afraid that false apostles, who disguise themselves as servants of Christ, will lead them away from the simplicity of the gospel. With irony, he compares himself to these men and lists his sufferings: beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, and his worry for the churches. He would rather boast about his weakness, such as when he escaped from Damascus in a basket.
sum.5: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain, because now is the time of salvation. He describes how he and his companions serve God with patience, truth, and love, even in the midst of suffering. Then he asks the Corinthians to open their hearts and turn away from whatever defiles, since they are the temple of the living God.
sum.9: Paul defends his authority against those who say he is bold in his letters but weak in person. He explains that the weapons he uses are not human but are powerful through God, and that he will be just as firm in person as he is by letter. He clarifies that he does not compare himself with others or boast about himself, since whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.
sum.2: Paul says that the believers in Corinth are a "letter from Christ," written by the Spirit on the heart, and that his ability as a minister comes from God. He contrasts the old covenant, which was of the letter, with the new covenant of the Spirit, which gives life and freedom. Those who look at the glory of the Lord are being transformed more and more into his likeness.
sum.11: Paul tells of a man who, fourteen years earlier, was caught up to paradise, but he says he would rather boast about his weaknesses. God did not take away his "thorn in the flesh," and told him, "My grace is sufficient for you," because his power is made perfect in weakness. Paul defends his authority and his love for the Corinthians, and he fears that he may find sin among them.
sum.12: Paul warns that he will come to Corinth for the third time and that he will not spare those who continue to sin. He asks them to examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith, because Christ lives in them. He writes to build them up, not to tear them down, and he closes by encouraging them to live in peace and unity, with a blessing.
sum.1: Paul explains that he wrote with tears, out of love, so that he would not have to come to the Corinthians in sorrow. He asks them to forgive and comfort the person who caused the pain, so that Satan does not take advantage of them. He describes his anxiety in Troas at not finding Titus. He gives thanks to God, who always leads him in triumph in Christ, and he speaks with sincerity.
sum.3: Paul says that, because of God's mercy, he does not lose heart when preaching Christ with truth, even though some do not see it because they are blinded. He explains that he carries the treasure of the gospel in "jars of clay," weak but held up by God's power. Although his body is wasting away, his inner self is being renewed, and he looks to what is eternal and cannot be seen.
sum.0: Paul and Timothy greet the church in Corinth and praise God, who comforts us in our troubles so that we can comfort others. Paul tells how, in Asia, he came close to death and learned to trust only in God, who raises the dead. He explains that he changed his travel plans in order to look after the Corinthians, and that God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.
sum.4: Paul says that even though our earthly body will wear out, God is preparing an eternal home for us in heaven. That is why we live by faith and seek to please him, knowing that we will all give an account before Christ. The love of Christ, who died for everyone, makes us new creations. God has reconciled us to himself and asks us to invite others: "Be reconciled to God."
sum.8: Paul encourages the Corinthians to have the gift they promised ready for the Christians in need, and he sends brothers to help them get it prepared. He teaches that God loves the person who gives with joy and willingness, and that God provides so that they may abound in every good work. Their generosity will supply the needs of others and will lead many to give thanks to God.
sum.6: Paul encourages the Corinthians to cleanse themselves from everything that defiles and to live in holiness, and he tells them that they hold a place in his heart. He shares that God comforted him with the arrival of Titus, who brought good news. He teaches that godly sorrow leads to a repentance that brings salvation, while the sorrow of the world brings death.
sum.7: Paul encourages the Corinthians to finish their collection for the needy believers, holding up the churches of Macedonia as an example. Though those churches were poor, they gave joyfully. He reminds them that Christ became poor to make us rich, and he asks them to give according to what they have, so that there is fairness. He sends Titus and other brothers to manage the gift with integrity.
